π⁡(A)=(π1​(A)00π2​(A))\pi(A)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\pi_{1}(A)&0\\ 0&\pi_{2}(A)\end{array}\right) (8)

Then the vector

Ψ=12​(Ψ1Ψ2)\Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\end{array}\right) (9)

satisfies the required relation

ω⁡(A)=⟨Ψ,π⁡(A)​Ψ⟩.\omega(A)=\left\langle\Psi,\pi(A)\Psi\right\rangle\ . (10)

For more information on operator algebras see [44, 5, 6].

In classical mechanics one has a similar structure. Here the algebra of observables is commutative and can be identified with the algebra of continuous functions on phase space. In addition, there is a second product, the Poisson bracket. This product is only densely defined. States are probability measures, and pure states correspond to the evaluation of functions at a given point of phase space.

3 Locally covariant field theory

Field theory involves infinitely many degrees of freedom, associated to the points of spacetime. Crucial for the success of field theory is a principle which regulates the way these degrees of freedom influence each other. This is the principle of locality, more precisely expressed by the German word Nahwirkungsprinzip. It states that each degree of freedom is influenced only by a relatively small number of other degrees of freedom. This induces a concept of neighborhoods in the set of degrees of freedom.

The original motivation for developing QFT was to combine the QM with special relativity. In this sense we expect to have in our theory some notion of causality. Let us briefly describe what it means in mathematical terms. In special relativity space and time are described together with one object, called Minkowski spacetime. Since it will be useful later on, we define now a general notion of a spacetime in physics.

Definition 3.1.

A spacetime (M,g)(M,g) is a smooth (4 dimensional) manifold (Hausdorff, paracompact, connected) with a smooth pseudo-Riemannian metric 44 4 a smooth tensor field g∈Γ⁡(T∗​M⊗T∗​M)g\in\Gamma(T^{*}M\otimes T^{*}M), s.t. for every p∈Mp\in M, gpg_{p} is a symmetric non degenerate bilinear form. of Lorentz signature (we choose the convention (+,−,−,−)(+,-,-,-)).

A spacetime MM is said to be orientable if there exists a differential form of maximal degree (a volume form), which does not vanish anywhere. We say that MM is time-orientable if there exists a smooth vector field uu on MM such that for ever p∈Mp\in M it holds g⁡(u,u)>0g(u,u)>0. We will always assume that our spacetimes are orientable and time-orientable. We fix the orientation and choose the time-orientation by selecting a specific vector field uu with the above property. Let γ:ℝ⊃I→M\gamma:\mathbb{R}\supset I\rightarrow M be a smooth curve in MM, for II an interval in ℝ\mathbb{R}. We say that γ\gamma is causal (timelike) if it holds g⁡(γ˙,γ˙)≥0g(\dot{\gamma},\dot{\gamma})\geq 0 (>0>0), where γ˙\dot{\gamma} is the vector tangent to the curve.

Given the global timelike vectorfield uu on MM, one calls a causal curve γ\gamma future-directed if g⁡(u,γ˙)>0g(u,\dot{\gamma})>0 all along γ\gamma, and analogously one calls γ\gamma past-directed if g⁡(u,γ˙)<0g(u,\dot{\gamma})<0. This induces a notion of time-direction in the spacetime (M,g)(M,g). For any point p∈Mp\in M, J±​(p)J^{\pm}(p) denotes the set of all points in MM which can be connected to xx by a future(+)/past(−)(-)-directed causal curve γ:I→M\gamma:I\to M so that x=γ⁡(infI)x=\gamma(\inf\,I). The set J+​(p)J^{+}(p) is called the causal future and J−​(p)J^{-}(p) the causal past of pp. The boundaries ∂J±​(p)\partial J^{\pm}(p) of these regions are called respectively: the future/past lightcone. Two subsets O1O_{1} and O2O_{2} in MM are called causally separated if they cannot be connected by a causal curve, i.e. if for all x∈O1¯x\in\overline{O_{1}}, J±​(x)J^{\pm}(x) has empty intersection with O2¯\overline{O_{2}}. By O⟂O^{\perp} we denote the causal complement of OO, i.e. the largest open set in MM which is causally separated from OO.

In the context of general relativity we will also make use of following definitions:

Definition 3.2.

A causal curve is future inextendible if there is no p∈Mp\in M such that:

∀U⊂M​open neighborhoods of ​p,∃t′​ s.t. ​γ​(t)∈U​∀t>t′.\forall U\subset M\mbox{open neighborhoods of }p,\,\exists t^{\prime}\textrm{ s.t. }\gamma(t)\in U\forall t>t^{\prime}\,.
Definition 3.3.

A Cauchy hypersurface in MM is a smooth subspace of MM such that every inextendible causal curve intersects it exactly once.

Definition 3.4.

An oriented and time-oriented spacetime MM is called globally hyperbolic if there exists a smooth foliation of MM by Cauchy hypersurfaces.

For now let us consider a simple case of the Minkowski spacetime 𝕄\mathbb{M} which is just ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} with the diagonal metric η=diag​(1,−1,−1,−1)\eta=\textrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1). A lightcone with apex pp is shown on figure 1, together with the future and past of pp.

One of the main principles of special relativity tells us that physical systems which are located in causally disjoint regions should in some sense be independent. Here we come to the important problem: How to implement this principle in quantum theory? A natural answer to this question is provided by the Haag-Kastler framework [27, 26], which is based on the principle of locality. In the previous section we argued that operator algebras are a natural framework for quantum physics. Locality can be realized by identifying the algebras of observables that can be measured in given bounded regions of spacetime. In other words we associate to each bounded 𝒪⊂M\mathcal{O}\subset M a C∗C^{*}-algebra 𝔄⁡(𝒪)\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}). This association has to be compatible with a physical notion of subsystems. It means that if we have a region 𝒪\mathcal{O} which lies inside 𝒪′\mathcal{O}^{\prime} we want the corresponding algebra 𝔄⁡(𝒪)\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}) to be contained inside 𝔄⁡(𝒪′)\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}^{\prime}), i.e. in a bigger region we have more observables. This property can be formulated as the Isotony condition for the net {𝔄⁡(𝒪)}\{\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O})\} of local algebras associated to bounded regions of the spacetime. In the Haag-Kastler framework one specializes to Minkowski space 𝕄\mathbb{M} and imposes some further, physically motivated, properties:

  • •

    Locality (Einstein causality). Algebras associated to spacelike separated regions commute: 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} spacelike separated from 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}, then [A,B]=0[A,B]=0, ∀A∈𝔄⁡(𝒪1)\forall A\in\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}_{1}), B∈𝔄⁡(𝒪2)B\in\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}_{2}). This expresses the “independence” of physical systems associated to regions 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} and 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2}.

  • •

    Covariance. The Minkowski spacetime has a large group of isometrics, namely the Poincaré group. We require that there exists a family of isomorphisms αL𝒪:𝔄⁡(𝒪)→𝔄⁡(L​𝒪)\alpha_{L}^{\mathcal{O}}:\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O})\rightarrow\mathfrak{A}(L\mathcal{O}) for Poincaré transformations LL, such that for 𝒪1⊂𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2} the restriction of αL𝒪2\alpha_{L}^{\mathcal{O}_{2}} to 𝔄⁡(𝒪1)\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) coincides with αL𝒪1\alpha_{L}^{\mathcal{O}_{1}} and such that: αL′L​𝒪∘αL𝒪=αL′​L𝒪\alpha^{L\mathcal{O}}_{L^{\prime}}\circ\alpha^{\mathcal{O}}_{L}=\alpha^{\mathcal{O}}_{L^{\prime}L},

  • •

    Time slice axiom: the algebra of a neighborhood of a Cauchy surface of a given region coincides with the algebra of the full region. Physically this correspond to a well-posedness of an initial value problem. We need to determine our observables in some small time interval (t0−ϵ,t0+ϵ)(t_{0}-\epsilon,t_{0}+\epsilon) to reconstruct the full algebra.

  • •

    Spectrum condition. This condition corresponds physically to the positivity of energy. One assumes that there exist a compatible family of faithful representations π𝒪\pi_{\mathcal{O}} of 𝔄⁡(𝒪)\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}) on a fixed Hilbert space (i.e. the restriction of π𝒪2\pi_{\mathcal{O}_{2}} to 𝔄⁡(𝒪1)\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) coincides with π𝒪1\pi_{\mathcal{O}_{1}} for 𝒪1⊂𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\mathcal{O}_{2}) such that translations are unitarily implemented, i.e. there is a unitary representation UU of the translation group satisfying

    U⁡(a)​π𝒪​(A)​U​(a)−1=π𝒪+a​(αa​(A)),A∈𝔄⁡(𝒪),U(a)\pi_{\mathcal{O}}(A)U(a)^{-1}=\pi_{\mathcal{O}+a}(\alpha_{a}(A))\ ,\ A\in\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{O}),

    and such that the joint spectrum of the generators PμP_{\mu} of translations ei​a​P=U⁡(a)e^{iaP}=U(a), a​P=aμ​PμaP=a^{\mu}P_{\mu}, is contained in the forward lightcone: σ⁡(P)⊂V¯+\sigma(P)\subset\overline{V}_{+}.

We now want to generalize this framework to theories on generic spacetimes. To start with, we may think of a globally hyperbolic neighborhood UU of a spacetime point xx in some spacetime MM. Moreover, we assume that any causal curve in MM with end points in UU lies entirely in UU. Then we require that the structure of the algebra of observables associated to UU should be completely independent of the world outside. We may formalize this idea by requiring that for any embedding χ:M→N\chi:M\to N of a globally hyperbolic manifold MM into another one NN which preserves the metric, the orientations and the causal structure55 5 The property of causality preserving is defined as follows: let χ:M→N\chi:M\to N, for any causal curve γ:[a,b]→N\gamma:[a,b]\to N, if γ⁡(a),γ⁡(b)∈χ⁡(M)\gamma(a),\gamma(b)\in\chi(M) then for all t∈]a,b[t\in]a,b[ we have: γ⁡(t)∈χ⁡(M)\gamma(t)\in\chi(M) . (these embeddings will be called admissible), there exist an injective homomorphism

αχ:𝔄⁡(M)→𝔄⁡(N)\alpha_{\chi}:\mathfrak{A}(M)\to\mathfrak{A}(N) (11)

of the corresponding algebras of observables, moreover if χ1:M→N\chi_{1}:M\to N and χ2:N→L\chi_{2}:N\to L are embeddings as above then we require the covariance relation

αχ2∘χ1=αχ2∘αχ1.\alpha_{\chi_{2}\circ\chi_{1}}=\alpha_{\chi_{2}}\circ\alpha_{\chi_{1}}\ . (12)

In this way we described a functor 𝔄\mathfrak{A} between two categories: the category 𝐋𝐨𝐜\mathrm{\mathbf{Loc}} of globally hyperbolic spacetimes with admissible embeddings as arrows and the category 𝐎𝐛𝐬\mathrm{\mathbf{Obs}} of algebras (Poisson algebras for classical physics and C*-algebras for quantum physics) with homomorphisms as arrows.

We may restrict the category of spacetimes to subregions of a given spacetime and the arrows to inclusions. In this way we obtain the Haag-Kastler net of local algebras on a globally hyperbolic spacetime as introduced by Dimock. In case the spacetime has nontrivial isometries, we obtain additional embeddings, and the covariance condition above provides a representation of the group of isometries by automorphisms of the Haag-Kastler net.

The causality requirements of the Haag-Kastler framework, i.e. the commutativity of observables localized in spacelike separated regions, is encoded in the general case in the tensor structure of the functor 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. Namely, the category of globally hyperbolic manifolds has the disjoint union as a tensor product, with the empty set as unit object and where admissible embeddings χ:M1⊗M2→N\chi:M_{1}\otimes M_{2}\to N have the property that the images χ⁡(M1)\chi(M_{1}) and χ⁡(M2)\chi(M_{2}) cannot be connected by a causal curve. On the level of C*-algebras we may use the minimal tensor product as a tensor structure. See [9] for details.

The solvability of the initial value problem can be formulated as the requirement that the algebra 𝔄⁡(N)\mathfrak{A}(N) of any neighborhood NN of some Cauchy surface Σ\Sigma already coincides with 𝔄⁡(M)\mathfrak{A}(M). This is the time slice axiom of axiomatic quantum field theory. It can be used to describe the evolution between different Cauchy surfaces. As a first step we associate to each Cauchy surface Σ\Sigma the inverse limit

𝔄⁡(Σ)=limN⊃Σ←𝔄⁡(N).\mathfrak{A}(\Sigma)=\lim^{\leftarrow}_{N\supset\Sigma}\mathfrak{A}(N)\ . (13)

Elements of the inverse limit consist of sequences A=(AN)LA⊃N⊃ΣA=(A_{N})_{L_{A}\supset N\supset\Sigma} with αN⊂K​(AN)=AK\alpha_{N\subset K}(A_{N})=A_{K}, K⊂LAK\subset L_{A}, with the equivalence relation

A∼B​ if ​AN=BN​ for all ​N⊂LA∩LB.A\sim B\text{ if }A_{N}=B_{N}\text{ for all }N\subset L_{A}\cap L_{B}\ . (14)

The algebra 𝔄⁡(Σ)\mathfrak{A}(\Sigma) can be embedded into 𝔄⁡(M)\mathfrak{A}(M) by

αΣ⊂M​(A)=αN⊂M​(AN)​ for some (and hence all) ​Σ⊂N⊂LA.\alpha_{\Sigma\subset M}(A)=\alpha_{N\subset M}(A_{N})\text{ for some (and hence all) }\Sigma\subset N\subset L_{A}\ . (15)

If we now adopt the time slice axiom we find that each homomorphism αN⊂M\alpha_{N\subset M} is an isomorphism. Hence αΣ⊂M\alpha_{\Sigma\subset M} is also an isomorphism and we obtain the propagator between two Cauchy surfaces Σ1\Sigma_{1} and Σ2\Sigma_{2} by

αΣ1​Σ2M=αΣ1⊂M−1∘αΣ2⊂M\alpha^{M}_{\Sigma_{1}\Sigma_{2}}=\alpha_{\Sigma_{1}\subset M}^{-1}\circ\alpha_{\Sigma_{2}\subset M} (16)

This construction resembles constructions in topological field theory for the description of cobordisms. But there one associates Hilbert spaces to components of the boundary and maps between these Hilbert spaces to the spacetime itself. This construction relies on the fact that for these theories the corresponding Hilbert spaces are finite dimensional. It was shown [55] that a corresponding construction for the free field in 3 and more dimensions does not work, since the corresponding Boboliubov transformation is not unitarily implementable (Shale’s criterion [48] is violated). Instead one may associate to the Cauchy surfaces the corresponding algebras of canonical commutation relations and to the cobordism an isomorphism between these algebras. For the algebra of canonical anticommutation relations for the free Dirac fields the above isomorphism was explicitly constructed [56]. Our general argument shows that the association of a cobordism between two Cauchy surfaces of globally hyperbolic spacetimes to an isomorphism of algebras always exists provided the time slice axiom is satisfied. As recently shown, the latter axiom is actually generally valid in perturbative Algebraic Quantum Field Theory [13].

In the Haag-Kastler framework on Minkowski space an essential ingredient was translation symmetry. This symmetry allowed the comparison of observables in different regions of spacetime and was (besides locality) a crucial input for the analysis of scattering states.

In the general covariant framework sketched above no comparable structure is available. Instead one may use fields which are subject to a suitable covariance condition, termed locally covariant fields. A locally covariant field is a family φM\varphi_{M} of fields on spacetimes MM such that for every embedding χ:M→N\chi:M\to N as above

αχ​(φM​(x))=φN​(χ⁡(x)).\alpha_{\chi}(\varphi_{M}(x))=\varphi_{N}(\chi(x))\ . (17)

If we consider fields as distributions with values in the algebras of observables, a field φ\varphi may be considered as a natural transformation between the functor 𝔇\mathfrak{D} of test function spaces to the functor 𝔄\mathfrak{A} of field theory. The functor 𝔇\mathfrak{D} associates to every spacetime MM its space of compactly supported 𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty}-functions,

𝔇⁡(M)=𝒞c∞​(M,ℝ),\mathfrak{D}(M)=\mathcal{C}^{\infty}_{\mathrm{c}}(M,\mathbb{R})\ , (18)

and to every embedding χ:M→N\chi:M\to N of spacetimes the pushforward of test functions f∈𝔇⁡(M)f\in\mathfrak{D}(M)

𝔇​χ≡χ∗,χ∗​f​(x)={f​(χ−1​(x)),x∈χ⁡(M)0, else\mathfrak{D}\chi\equiv\chi_{*}\ ,\ \chi_{*}f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}f(\chi^{-1}(x))&,&x\in\chi(M)\\ 0&,&\text{ else}\end{array}\right. (19)

𝔇\mathfrak{D} is a covariant functor. Its target category is the category of locally convex vector spaces 𝐕𝐞𝐜\mathrm{\mathbf{Vec}} which contains also the category of topological algebras which is the target category for 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. A natural transformation φ:𝔇→𝔄\varphi:\mathfrak{D}\to\mathfrak{A} between covariant functors with the same source and target categories is a family of morphisms φM:𝔇⁡(M)→𝔄⁡(M)\varphi_{M}:\mathfrak{D}(M)\to\mathfrak{A}(M), M∈Obj⁡(𝐋𝐨𝐜)M\in\mathrm{Obj}(\mathrm{\mathbf{Loc}}) such that

𝔄​χ∘φM=φN∘𝔇​χ\mathfrak{A}\chi\circ\varphi_{M}=\varphi_{N}\circ\mathfrak{D}\chi (20)

with 𝔄​χ=αχ\mathfrak{A}\chi=\alpha_{\chi}.

4 Classical field theory

Before we enter the arena of quantum field theory we show that the concept of local covariance leads to a nice reformulation of classical field theory in which the relation to QFT becomes clearly visible. Let us consider a scalar field theory. On a given spacetime MM the possible field configurations are the smooth functions on MM. If we embed a spacetime MM into another spacetime NN, the field configurations on NN can be pulled back to MM, and we obtain a functor 𝔈\mathfrak{E} from 𝐋𝐨𝐜\mathrm{\mathbf{Loc}} to the category 𝐕𝐞𝐜\mathrm{\mathbf{Vec}} of locally convex vector spaces

𝔈⁡(M)=𝒞∞​(M,ℝ),𝔈​χ=χ∗\mathfrak{E}(M)=\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(M,\mathbb{R})\ ,\ \mathfrak{E}\chi=\chi^{*} (21)

with the pullback χ∗​φ=φ∘χ\chi^{*}\varphi=\varphi\circ\chi for φ∈𝒞∞​(M,ℝ)\varphi\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(M,\mathbb{R}). Note that 𝔈\mathfrak{E} is contravariant, whereas the functor 𝔇\mathfrak{D} of test function spaces with compact support is covariant.

The classical observables are real valued functions on 𝔈⁡(M)\mathfrak{E}(M), i.e. (not necessarily linear) functionals. An important property of a functional is its spacetime support. Is is defined as a generalization of the distributional support, namely as the set of points x∈Mx\in M such that FF depends on the field configuration in any neighbourhood of xx.

suppF≐{\displaystyle\mathrm{supp}\,F\doteq\{ x∈M|∀ neighbourhoods ​U​ of ​x​∃φ,ψ∈𝔈⁡(M),supp​ψ⊂U\displaystyle x\in M|\forall\text{ neighbourhoods }U\text{ of }x\ \exists\varphi,\psi\in\mathfrak{E}(M),\mathrm{supp}\,\psi\subset U (22)
such that F(φ+ψ)≠F(φ)}.\displaystyle\text{ such that }F(\varphi+\psi)\not=F(\varphi)\}\ .

Here we will discuss only compactly supported functionals. Next one has to select a class of functionals which are sufficiently regular such that all mathematical operations one wants to perform are meaningful and which on the other side is large enough to cover the interesting cases.

One class one may consider is the class 𝔉reg​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{reg}}(M) of regular polynomials

F⁡(φ)=∑finite∫d​x1​…​d​xn​fn​(x1,…,xn)​φ​(x1)​…​φ​(xn)F(\varphi)=\sum_{\text{finite}}\int dx_{1}\dots dx_{n}f_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\varphi(x_{1})\dots\varphi(x_{n}) (23)

with test functions fn∈𝔇⁡(Mn)f_{n}\in\mathfrak{D}(M^{n}). Another class 𝔉loc​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M) consists of the local functionals

F⁡(φ)=∫d​x​ℒ​(x,φ⁡(x),∂φ⁡(x),…)F(\varphi)=\int dx\mathcal{L}(x,\varphi(x),\partial\varphi(x),\dots) (24)

where ℒ\mathcal{L} depends smoothly on xx and on finitely many derivatives of φ\varphi at xx. The local functionals arise as actions and induce the dynamics. The only regular polynomials in this class are the linear functionals

F⁡(φ)=∫d​x​f​(x)​φ​(x).F(\varphi)=\int dxf(x)\varphi(x)\ . (25)

It turns out to be convenient to characterize the admissible class of functionals in terms of their functional derivatives.

Definition 4.1 (after [40]).

Let XX and YY be topological vector spaces, U⊆XU\subseteq X an open set and f:U→Yf:U\rightarrow Y a map. The derivative of ff at xx in the direction of hh is defined as

d​f​(x)​(h)≐limt→01t​(f⁡(x+t​h)−f⁡(x))df(x)(h)\doteq\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{t}\left(f(x+th)-f(x)\right) (26)

whenever the limit exists. The function ff is called differentiable at xx if d​f​(x)​(h)df(x)(h) exists for all h∈Xh\in X. It is called continuously differentiable if it is differentiable at all points of UU and d​f:U×X→Y,(x,h)↦d​f​(x)​(h)df:U\times X\rightarrow Y,(x,h)\mapsto df(x)(h) is a continuous map. It is called a 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-map if it is continuous and continuously differentiable. Higher derivatives are defined for 𝒞n\mathcal{C}^{n}-maps by

dn​f​(x)​(h1,…,hn)≐limt→01t​(dn−1​f​(x+t​hn)​(h1,…,hn−1)−dn−1​f​(x)​(h1,…,hn−1))d^{n}f(x)(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n})\doteq\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{t}\big(d^{n-1}f(x+th_{n})(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n-1})-d^{n-1}f(x)(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n-1})\big) (27)

In particular it means that if FF is a smooth functional on 𝔈⁡(M)\mathfrak{E}(M), then its nn-th derivative at the point φ∈𝔈⁡(M)\varphi\in\mathfrak{E}(M) is a compactly supported distributional density F(n)​(φ)∈ℰ′​(Mn)F^{(n)}(\varphi)\in\mathcal{E}^{\prime}(M^{n}). There is a distinguished volume form on MM, namely the one provided by the metric: −det​(g)​d4​x\sqrt{-\textrm{det}(g)}d^{4}x. We can use it to construct densities from functions and to provide an embedding of 𝒟⁡(Mn)\mathcal{D}(M^{n}) into ℰ′​(Mn)\mathcal{E}^{\prime}(M^{n}). For more details on distributions on manifolds, see chapter 1 of [2]. Using the distinguished volume form we can identify derivatives F(n)​(φ)F^{(n)}(\varphi) with distributions. We further need some conditions on their wave front sets.

Let us make a brief excursion to the concept of wave front sets and its use for the treatment of distributions. Readers less familiar with these topics can find more details in the appendix A or refer to [35] or chapter 4 of [1]. Let t∈𝒟′​(ℝn)t\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and f∈𝒟⁡(ℝn)f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). The Fourier transform of the product f​tft is a smooth function. If this function vanishes fast at infinity for all f∈𝒟⁡(ℝn)f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), tt itself is a smooth function. Singularities of tt show up in the absence of fast decay in some directions. A point (x,k)∈ℝn×(ℝn∖{0})(x,k)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}) is called a regular point of tt if there exists a test function ff with f⁡(x)=1f(x)=1 such that the Fourier transform of f​tft decays strongly in an open cone around kk. The wave front set of tt is now defined as the complement of the set of regular points of tt in ℝn×(ℝn∖{0})\mathbb{R}^{n}\times(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}).

On a manifold MM the definition of the Fourier transform depends on the choice of a chart. But the property of strong decay in some direction (characterized now by a point (x,k)(x,k), k≠0k\not=0 of the cotangent bundle T∗​MT^{*}M) turns out to be independent of the chart. Therefore the wave front set WF\mathrm{WF} of a distribution on a manifold MM is a well defined closed conical subset of the cotangent bundle (with the zero section removed).

Let us illustrate the concept of the wave front set in two examples. The first one is the δ\delta-function. We find

∫d​x​f​(x)​δ​(x)​ei​k​x=f⁡(0),\int dxf(x)\delta(x)e^{ikx}=f(0)\ , (28)

hence WF⁡(δ)={(0,k),k≠0}\mathrm{WF}(\delta)=\{(0,k),k\not=0\}.

The other one is the function x↦(x+i​ϵ)−1x\mapsto(x+i\epsilon)^{-1} in the limit ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow 0. We have

limϵ↓0∫dxf⁡(x)x+i​ϵei​k​x=−i∫k∞dk′f^(k′).\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\int dx\frac{f(x)}{x+i\epsilon}e^{ikx}=-i\int_{k}^{\infty}dk^{\prime}\hat{f}(k^{\prime})\ . (29)

Since the Fourier transform f^\hat{f} of a test function f∈𝒟⁡(ℝ)f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}) is strongly decaying for k→∞k\to\infty, ∫k∞d​k′​f^​(k′)\int_{k}^{\infty}dk^{\prime}\hat{f}(k^{\prime}) is strongly decaying for k→∞k\to\infty, but for k→−∞k\to-\infty we obtain

limk→−∞∫k∞d​k′​f^​(k′)=2​π​f​(0),\lim_{k\to-\infty}\int_{k}^{\infty}dk^{\prime}\hat{f}(k^{\prime})=2\pi f(0)\ , (30)

hence

WF⁡(limϵ↓0(x+i​ϵ)−1)={(0,k),k<0}.\mathrm{WF}(\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}(x+i\epsilon)^{-1})=\{(0,k),k<0\}\ . (31)

The wave front sets provide a simple criterion for the pointwise multiplicability of distributions. Namely, let t,st,s be distributions on an nn dimensional manifold MM such that the pointwise sum (Whitney sum) of their wave front sets

WF(t)+WF(s)={(x,k+k′)|(x,k)∈WF(t),(x,k′)∈WF(s)}\mathrm{WF}(t)+\mathrm{WF}(s)=\{(x,k+k^{\prime})|(x,k)\in\mathrm{WF}(t),(x,k^{\prime})\in\mathrm{WF}(s)\} (32)

does not intersect the zero section of T∗​MT^{*}M. Then the pointwise product t​sts can be defined by

⟨t​s,f​g⟩=1(2​π)n​∫d​k​t​f^​(k)​s​g^​(−k)\langle ts,fg\rangle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int dk\,\widehat{tf}(k)\widehat{sg}(-k) (33)

for test functions ff and gg with sufficiently small support and where the Fourier transform refers to an arbitrary chart covering the supports of ff and gg. The convergence of the integral on the right hand side follows from the fact, that for every k≠0k\not=0 either t​f^\widehat{tf} decays fast in a conical neighborhood around kk or s​g^\widehat{sg} decays fast in a conical neighborhood around −k-k whereas the other factor is polynomially bounded.

The other crucial property is the characterization of the propagation of singularities. To understand it in more physical terms it is useful to use an analogy with Hamiltonian mechanics. Note that the cotangent bundle T∗​MT^{*}M has a natural symplectic structure. The symplectic 2-form is defined as an exterior derivative of the canonical one-form, given in local coordinates as θ(x,k)=∑𝔦=1nki​d​xi\theta_{(x,{k})}=\sum_{{\mathfrak{i}}=1}^{n}{k}_{i}dx^{i} (ki{k}_{i} are coordinates in the fibre). Let PP be a partial differential operator with real principal symbol σP\sigma_{P}. Note that σP\sigma_{P} is a function on T∗​MT^{*}M and its differential d​σPd\sigma_{P} is a 1-form. On a symplectic manifold 1-forms can be canonically identified with vector fields by means of the symplectic form. Therefore every differentiable function HH determines a unique vector field XHX_{H}, called the Hamiltonian vector field with the Hamiltonian HH. Let XPX_{P} be the Hamiltonian vector field corresponding to σP\sigma_{P}. Explicitly it can be written as:

XP=∑i=1n∂σP∂kj​∂∂xj−∂σP∂xj​∂∂kjX_{P}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial\sigma_{P}}{\partial{k}_{j}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{j}}-\frac{\partial\sigma_{P}}{\partial x_{j}}\frac{\partial}{\partial{k}_{j}}

Let us now consider the integral curves (Hamiltonian flow) of this vector field. A curve (xj​(t),kj​(t))(x_{j}(t),{k}_{j}(t)) is an integral curve of XPX_{P} if it fulfills the system of equations (Hamilton’s equations):

d​xjd​t\displaystyle\frac{dx_{j}}{dt} =∂σP∂kj,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\sigma_{P}}{\partial{k}_{j}}\,,
d​kjd​t\displaystyle\frac{d{k}_{j}}{dt} =−∂σP∂xj.\displaystyle=-\frac{\partial\sigma_{P}}{\partial x_{j}}\,.

The set of all such solution curves is called the bicharacteristic flow. Along the Hamiltonian flow it holds d​σPd​t=XP​(σP)=0\frac{d\sigma_{P}}{dt}=X_{P}(\sigma_{P})=0 (this is the law of conservation of energy for autonomous systems in classical mechanics), so σP\sigma_{P} is constant under the bicharacteristic flow. If σP​((xj​(t),kj​(t)))=0\sigma_{P}((x_{j}(t),{k}_{j}(t)))=0 we call the corresponding flow null. The set of all such integral curves is called the null bicharacteristics.

Let us now define the characteristics of PP as char​P={(x,k)∈T∗​M|σ⁡(P)​(x,k)=0}\mathrm{char}P=\{(x,k)\in T^{*}M|\sigma(P)(x,k)=0\} of PP. Then the theorem on the propagation of singularities states that the wave front set of a solution uu of the equation P​u=fPu=f with ff smooth is a union of orbits of the Hamiltonian flow XPX_{P} on the characteristics char​P\mathrm{char}P.

In field theory on Lorentzian spacetime we are mainly interested in hyperbolic differential operators. Their characteristics is the light cone, and the principal symbol is the metric on the cotangent bundle. The wave front set of solutions therefore is a union of null geodesics together with their cotangent vectors k=g⁡(γ˙,⋅)k=g(\dot{\gamma},\cdot).

We already have all the kinematical structures we need. Now in order to specify a concrete physical model we need to introduce the dynamics. This can be done by means of a generalized Lagrangian. As the name suggests the idea is motivated by Lagrangian mechanics. Indeed, we can think of this formalism as a way to make precise the variational calculus in field theory. Note that since our spacetimes are globally hyperbolic, they are never compact. Moreover we cannot restrict ourselves to compactly supported field configurations, since the nontrivial solutions of globally hyperbolic equations don’t belong to this class. Therefore we cannot identify the action with a functional on 𝔈⁡(M)\mathfrak{E}(M) obtained by integrating the Lagrangian density over the whole manifold. Instead we follow [12] and define a Lagrangian LL as a natural transformation between the functor of test function spaces 𝔇\mathfrak{D} and the functor 𝔉loc\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{loc}} such that it satisfies supp⁡(LM​(f))⊆supp⁡(f)\mathrm{supp}(L_{M}(f))\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(f) and the additivity rule 66 6 We do not require linearity since in quantum field theory the renormalization flow does not preserve the linear structure; it respects, however, the additivity rule (see [12]).

LM​(f+g+h)=LM​(f+g)−LM​(g)+LM​(g+h),L_{M}(f+g+h)=L_{M}(f+g)-L_{M}(g)+L_{M}(g+h)\,,

for f,g,h∈𝔇⁡(M)f,g,h\in\mathfrak{D}(M) and supp​f∩supp​h=∅\mathrm{supp}\,f\cap\mathrm{supp}\,h=\varnothing. The action S⁡(L)S(L) is now defined as an equivalence class of Lagrangians [12], where two Lagrangians L1,L2L_{1},L_{2} are called equivalent L1∼L2L_{1}\sim L_{2} if

supp⁡(L1,M−L2,M)​(f)⊂supp​d​f,\mathrm{supp}(L_{1,M}-L_{2,M})(f)\subset\mathrm{supp}\,df\,, (34)

for all spacetimes MM and all f∈𝔇⁡(M)f\in\mathfrak{D}(M). This equivalence relation allows us to identify Lagrangians differing by a total divergence. For the free minimally coupled (i.e. ξ=0\xi=0) scalar field the generalized Lagrangian is given by:

LM​(f)​(φ)=12​∫M(∇μφ​∇μφ−m2​φ2)​f​dvolM.L_{M}(f)(\varphi)=\frac{1}{2}\int\limits_{M}(\nabla_{\mu}\varphi\nabla^{\mu}\varphi-m^{2}\varphi^{2})f\,\mathrm{dvol}_{\scriptscriptstyle{M}}\,. (35)

The equations of motion are to be understood in the sense of [12]. Concretely, the Euler-Lagrange derivative of SS is a natural transformation S′:𝔈→𝔇′S^{\prime}:\mathfrak{E}\to\mathfrak{D}^{\prime} defined as

⟨SM′​(φ),h⟩=⟨LM​(f)(1)​(φ),h⟩,\left<S^{\prime}_{M}(\varphi),h\right>=\left<L_{M}(f)^{(1)}(\varphi),h\right>\,, (36)

with f≡1f\equiv 1 on supp​h\mathrm{supp}h. The field equation is now a condition on φ\varphi:

SM′​(φ)=0.S_{M}^{\prime}(\varphi)=0\,. (37)

Note that the way we obtained the field equation is analogous to variational calculus on finite dimensional spaces. We can push this analogy even further and think of variation of a functional in a direction in configuration space given by an infinite dimensional vector field. This concept is well understood in mathematics and for details one can refer for example to [40, 39]. Here we consider only variations in the directions of compactly supported configurations, so the space of vector fields we are interested in can be identified with 𝔙(M)={X:𝔈(M)→𝔇(M)|X smooth}\mathfrak{V}(M)=\{X:\mathfrak{E}(M)\to\mathfrak{D}(M)|X\text{ smooth}\}. In more precise terms this is the space of vector fields on 𝔈⁡(M)\mathfrak{E}(M), considered as a manifold77 7 An infinite dimensional manifold is modeled on a locally convex vector space just as a finite dimensional one is modeled on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. For more details see [40, 39]. modeled over 𝔇⁡(M)\mathfrak{D}(M). The set of functionals

φ↦⟨SM′​(φ),X⁡(φ)⟩,X∈𝔙⁡(M)\varphi\mapsto\langle S_{M}^{\prime}(\varphi),X(\varphi)\rangle\ ,\ X\in\mathfrak{V}(M) (38)

is an ideal ℑS​(M)\mathfrak{I}_{S}(M) of 𝔉⁡(M)\mathfrak{F}(M) with respect to pointwise multiplication,

(F⋅G)​(φ)=F⁡(φ)​G​(φ).(F\cdot G)(\varphi)=F(\varphi)G(\varphi)\ . (39)

The quotient

𝔉S​(M)=𝔉⁡(M)/ℑS​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{S}(M)=\mathfrak{F}(M)/\mathfrak{I}_{S}(M) (40)

can be interpreted as the space of solutions of the field equation. The latter can be identified with the phase space of the classical field theory.

We now want to equip 𝔉S​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{S}(M) with a Poisson bracket. Here we rely on a method originally introduced by Peierls. Peierls considers the influence of an additional term in the action. Let F∈𝔉loc​(M)F\in\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M) be a local functional. We are interested in the flow (Φλ)(\Phi_{\lambda}) on 𝔈⁡(M)\mathfrak{E}(M) which deforms solutions of the original field equation SM′​(φ)=ωS_{M}^{\prime}(\varphi)=\omega with a given source term ω\omega to those of the perturbed equation SM′​(φ)+λ​F(1)​(φ)=ωS_{M}^{\prime}(\varphi)+\lambda F^{(1)}(\varphi)=\omega. Let Φ0​(φ)=φ\Phi_{0}(\varphi)=\varphi and

dd​λ​(SM′​(Φλ​(φ))+F(1)​(Φλ​(φ)))|λ=0=0.\frac{d}{d\lambda}\left.\left(S_{M}^{\prime}(\Phi_{\lambda}(\varphi))+F^{(1)}(\Phi_{\lambda}(\varphi))\right)\right|_{\lambda=0}=0\ . (41)

Note that the second variational derivative of the unperturbed action induces an operator SM′′​(φ):𝔈⁡(M)→𝔇′​(M)S^{\prime\prime}_{M}(\varphi):\mathfrak{E}(M)\rightarrow\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}(M). We define it in the following way:

⟨SM′′​(φ),h1⊗h2⟩≐⟨LM(2)​(f)​(φ),h1⊗h2⟩,\left<S^{\prime\prime}_{M}(\varphi),h_{1}\otimes h_{2}\right>\doteq\left<L^{(2)}_{M}(f)(\varphi),h_{1}\otimes h_{2}\right>\,,

where f≡1f\equiv 1 on the supports of h1h_{1} and h2h_{2}. This defines SM′′​(φ)S^{\prime\prime}_{M}(\varphi) as an element of 𝔇′​(M2)\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}(M^{2}) and by Schwartz’s kernel theorem we can associate to it an operator from 𝔇⁡(M)\mathfrak{D}(M) to 𝔇′​(M)\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}(M). Actually, since LM​(f)L_{M}(f) is local, the second derivative has support on the diagonal, so SM′′​(φ)S^{\prime\prime}_{M}(\varphi) can be evaluated on smooth functions h1h_{1}, h2h_{2}, where only one of them is required to be compactly supported, and it induces an operator (the so called linearized Euler-Lagrange operator) E′​[SM]​(φ):𝔈⁡(M)→𝔇′​(M)E^{\prime}[S_{M}](\varphi):\mathfrak{E}(M)\rightarrow\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}(M).

From (41) it follows that the vector field φ↦X⁡(φ)=dd​λ​Φλ​(φ)|λ=0\varphi\mapsto X(\varphi)=\frac{d}{d\lambda}\Phi_{\lambda}(\varphi)|_{\lambda=0} satisfies the equation

⟨SM′′(φ),X(φ)⊗⋅⟩+⟨F(1)(φ),⋅⟩=0,\left<S^{\prime\prime}_{M}(\varphi),X(\varphi)\otimes\cdot\right>+\left<F^{(1)}(\varphi),\cdot\right>=0\,, (42)

which in a different notation can be written as

⟨E′​[SM]​(φ),X⁡(φ)⟩+F(1)​(φ)=0.\left<E^{\prime}[S_{M}](\varphi),X(\varphi)\right>+F^{(1)}(\varphi)=0\,.

We now assume that E′​[SM]​(φ)E^{\prime}[S_{M}](\varphi) is, for all φ\varphi, a normal hyperbolic differential operator 𝔈⁡(M)→𝔈⁡(M)\mathfrak{E}(M)\rightarrow\mathfrak{E}(M), and let ΔSR,ΔSA\Delta_{S}^{R},\Delta_{S}^{A} be the retarded and advanced Green’s operators, i.e. linear operators 𝔇⁡(M)→𝔈⁡(M)\mathfrak{D}(M)\rightarrow\mathfrak{E}(M) satisfying:

E′​[SM]∘ΔSR/A\displaystyle E^{\prime}[S_{M}]\circ\Delta^{R/A}_{S} =id𝔇⁡(M),\displaystyle=\mathrm{id}_{\mathfrak{D}(M)}\,,
ΔSR/A∘(E′​[SM]|𝔇⁡(M))\displaystyle\Delta^{R/A}_{S}\circ(E^{\prime}[S_{M}]\big|_{\mathfrak{D}(M)}) =id𝔇⁡(M).\displaystyle=\mathrm{id}_{\mathfrak{D}(M)}\,.

Moreover, with the use of Schwartz’s kernel theorem one can identify ΔSR/A:𝔇⁡(M)→𝔈⁡(M)\Delta^{R/A}_{S}:\mathfrak{D}(M)\rightarrow\mathfrak{E}(M) with elements of 𝒟′​(M2)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(M^{2}). As such, they are required to satisfy the following support properties:

supp⁡(ΔR)\displaystyle\mathrm{supp}(\Delta^{R}) ⊂{(x,y)∈M2|y∈J−​(x)},\displaystyle\subset\{(x,y)\in M^{2}|y\in J^{-}(x)\}\,, (43)
supp⁡(ΔA)\displaystyle\mathrm{supp}(\Delta^{A}) ⊂{(x,y)∈M2|y∈J+​(x)}.\displaystyle\subset\{(x,y)\in M^{2}|y\in J^{+}(x)\}\,. (44)

Their difference ΔS=ΔSA−ΔSR\Delta_{S}=\Delta_{S}^{\rm A}-\Delta_{S}^{\rm R} is called the causal propagator of the Klein-Gordon equation. Coming back to equation (42) we have now two distinguished solutions for XX,

XR,A​(φ)=ΔSR,A​F(1)​(φ).X^{R,A}(\varphi)=\Delta_{S}^{R,A}F^{(1)}(\varphi)\ . (45)

The difference of the associated derivations on 𝔉⁡(M)\mathfrak{F}(M) defines a product

{F,G}S​(φ)=⟨ΔS​(φ)​F(1)​(φ),G(1)​(φ)⟩\{F,G\}_{S}(\varphi)=\langle\Delta_{S}(\varphi)F^{(1)}(\varphi),G^{(1)}(\varphi)\rangle (46)

on 𝔉loc​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M), the so-called Peierls bracket.

The Peierls bracket satisfies the conditions of a Poisson bracket, in particular the Jacobi identity (for a simple proof see [36]). Moreover, if one of the entries is in the ideal ℑS​(M)\mathfrak{I}_{S}(M), also the bracket is in the ideal, hence the Peierls bracket induces a Poisson bracket on the quotient algebra.

In standard cases, the Peierls bracket coincides with the canonical Poisson bracket. Namely let

ℒ⁡(φ)=12​∂μφ​∂μφ−m22​φ2−λ4!​φ4.\mathcal{L}(\varphi)=\frac{1}{2}\partial^{\mu}\varphi\partial_{\mu}\varphi-\frac{m^{2}}{2}\varphi^{2}-\frac{\lambda}{4!}\varphi^{4}\ . (47)

Then SM′​(φ)=−((□+m2)​φ+λ3!​φ3)S^{\prime}_{M}(\varphi)=-\left((\square+m^{2})\varphi+\frac{\lambda}{3!}\varphi^{3}\right) and SM′′​(φ)S_{M}^{\prime\prime}(\varphi) is the linear operator

−(□+m2+λ2​φ2)-\left(\square+m^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\varphi^{2}\right) (48)

(the last term acts as a multiplication operator).

The Peierls bracket is

{φ⁡(x),φ⁡(y)}S=ΔS​(φ)​(x,y)\{\varphi(x),\varphi(y)\}_{S}=\Delta_{S}(\varphi)(x,y) (49)

where x↦ΔS​(φ)​(x,y)x\mapsto\Delta_{S}(\varphi)(x,y) is a solution of the (at φ\varphi) linearized equation of motion with the initial conditions

ΔS​(φ)​(y0,𝐱,y)=0,∂∂x0​ΔS​(φ)​(y0,𝐱,y)=δ⁡(𝐱,𝐲).\Delta_{S}(\varphi)(y^{0},\mathbf{x};y)=0\ ,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{0}}\Delta_{S}(\varphi)(y^{0},\mathbf{x};y)=\delta(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\ . (50)

This coincides with the Poisson bracket in the canonical formalism. Namely, let φ\varphi be a solution of the field equation. Then

OPEN0={(□+m2)​φ​(x)+λ3!​φ3​(x),φ⁡(y)}=(□+m2+λ2​φ​(x)2))​{φ⁡(x),φ⁡(y)}0=\{(\square+m^{2})\varphi(x)+\frac{\lambda}{3!}\varphi^{3}(x),\varphi(y)\}=(\square+m^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\varphi(x)^{2}))\{\varphi(x),\varphi(y)\} (51)

hence the Poisson bracket satisfies the linearized field equation with the same initial conditions as the Peierls bracket.

Let us now discuss the domain of definition of the Peierls bracket. It turns out that it is a larger class of functionals than just 𝔉loc​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M). To identify this class we use the fact that the WF set of ΔS\Delta_{S} is given by

WF⁡(ΔS)={(x,k,x′,−k′)∈T˙∗​M2|(x,k)∼(x′,k′)},\mathrm{WF}(\Delta_{S})=\{(x,k;x^{\prime},-k^{\prime})\in\dot{T}^{*}M^{2}|(x,k)\sim(x^{\prime},k^{\prime})\}\,,

where the equivalence relation ∼\sim means that there exists a null geodesic strip such that both (x,k)(x,k) and (x′,k′)(x^{\prime},k^{\prime}) belong to it. A null geodesic strip is a curve in T∗​MT^{*}M of the form (γ⁡(λ),k⁡(λ))(\gamma(\lambda),k(\lambda)), λ∈I⊂ℝ\lambda\in I\subset\mathbb{R}, where γ⁡(λ)\gamma(\lambda) is a null geodesic parametrized by λ\lambda and k⁡(λ)k(\lambda) is given by k​(λ)=g​(γ˙​(λ),⋅)k(\lambda)=g(\dot{\gamma}(\lambda),\cdot). This follows from the theorem on the propagation of singularities together with the initial conditions and the antisymmetry of ΔS\Delta_{S}. (See [43] for a detailed argument.)

It is now easy to check, using Hörmander’s criterion on the multiplicability of distributions [35] that the Peierls bracket (46) is well defined if FF and GG are such that the sum of the WF sets of the functional derivatives F(1)​(φ),G(1)​(φ)∈ℰ′​(M)F^{(1)}(\varphi),G^{(1)}(\varphi)\in\mathcal{E}^{\prime}(M) and Δ∈𝒟′​(M2)\Delta\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(M^{2}) don’t intersect the 0-section of the cotangent bundle T∗​M2T^{*}M^{2}. This is the case if the functionals fulfill the following criterion:

WF⁡(F(n)​(φ))⊂Ξn,∀n∈ℕ,∀φ∈𝔈⁡(M),\mathrm{WF}(F^{(n)}(\varphi))\subset\Xi_{n},\quad\forall n\in\mathbb{N},\ \forall\varphi\in\mathfrak{E}(M)\,, (52)

where Ξn\Xi_{n} is an open cone defined as

Ξn≐T∗​Mn∖{(x1,…,xn,k1,…,kn)|(k1,…,kn)∈(V¯+n∪V¯−n)(x1,…,xn)},\Xi_{n}\doteq T^{*}M^{n}\setminus\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{n};k_{1},\dots,k_{n})|(k_{1},\dots,k_{n})\in(\overline{V}_{+}^{n}\cup\overline{V}_{-}^{n})_{(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})}\}\,, (53)

where (V¯±)x(\overline{V}_{\pm})_{x} is the closed future/past lightcone understood as a conic subset of Tx∗​MT^{*}_{x}M. We denote the space of smooth compactly supported functionals, satisfying (52) by 𝔉μ​c​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M) and call them microcausal functionals. This includes in particular local functionals. For them the support of the functional derivatives is on the thin diagonal, and the wave front sets satisfy ∑ki=0\sum k_{i}=0.

To see that {.,.}S\{.,.\}_{S} is indeed well defined on 𝔉μ​c​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M), note that WF⁡(Δ)\mathrm{WF}(\Delta) consists of elements (x,x′,k,k′)(x,x^{\prime},k,k^{\prime}), where kk, k′k^{\prime} are dual to lightlike vectors in Tx​MT_{x}M, Tx′​MT_{x^{\prime}}M accordingly. On the other hand, if (x,k1)∈WF⁡(F(1)​(φ))(x,k_{1})\in\mathrm{WF}(F^{(1)}(\varphi)), then k1k_{1} is necessarily dual to a vector which is spacelike, so k1+kk_{1}+k cannot be 0. The same argument is valid for G(1)​(φ)G^{(1)}(\varphi). Moreover it can be shown that {F,G}S∈𝔉μ​c​(M)\{F,G\}_{S}\in\mathfrak{F}_{{\mu\mathrm{c}}}(M). The classical field theory is defined as 𝔄(M)=(𝔉μ​c(M),{.,.}S)\mathfrak{A}(M)=(\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M),\{.,.\}_{S}). One can check that 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is indeed a covariant functor from 𝐋𝐨𝐜\mathrm{\mathbf{Loc}} to 𝐎𝐛𝐬\mathrm{\mathbf{Obs}}, the category of Poisson algebras.

5 Deformation quantization of free field theories

Starting from the Poisson algebra (𝔉μ​c(M),{.,.}S)(\mathfrak{F}_{{\mu\mathrm{c}}}(M),\{.,.\}_{S}) one may try to construct an associative algebra (𝔉μ​c​(M)​[[ℏ]],⋆)(\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M)[[\hbar]],\star) such that for ℏ→0\hbar\to 0

F⋆G→F⋅GF\star G\to F\cdot G (54)

and

[F,G]⋆/i​ℏ→{F,G}S.[F,G]_{\star}/i\hbar\to\{F,G\}_{S}\ . (55)

For the Poisson algebra of functions on a finite dimensional Poisson manifold the deformation quantization exists in the sense of formal power series due to a theorem of Kontsevich [38]. In field theory the formulas of Kontsevich lead to ill defined terms, and a general solution of the problem is not known. But in case the action is quadratic in the fields, the ⋆\star-product can be explicitly defined by

(F⋆G)​(φ)≐∑n=0∞ℏnn!​⟨F(n)​(φ),(i2​ΔS)⊗n​G(n)​(φ)⟩,(F\star G)(\varphi)\doteq\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\hbar^{n}}{n!}\left<F^{(n)}(\varphi),\left(\tfrac{i}{2}\Delta_{S}\right)^{\otimes n}G^{(n)}(\varphi)\right>\,, (56)

which can be formally written as ei​ℏ2​⟨ΔS,δ2δ​φ​δ​φ′⟩​F​(φ)​G​(φ′)|φ′=φe^{\frac{i\hbar}{2}\left\langle\Delta_{S},\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta\varphi\delta\varphi^{\prime}}\right\rangle}F(\varphi)G(\varphi^{\prime})|_{\varphi^{\prime}=\varphi}. This product is well defined (in the sense of formal power series in ℏ\hbar) for regular functionals F,G∈𝔉reg​(M)F,G\in\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{reg}}(M) and satisfies the conditions above. Let for instance

F⁡(φ)=e∫d​x​φ​(x)​f​(x),G⁡(φ)=e∫d​x​φ​(x)​g​(x),F(\varphi)=e^{\int dx\varphi(x)f(x)}\ ,\ G(\varphi)=e^{\int dx\varphi(x)g(x)}\ , (57)

with test functions f,g∈𝔇⁡(M)f,g\in\mathfrak{D}(M). We have

δnφ⁡(x1)​…​φ​(xn)​F​(φ)=f⁡(x1)​…​f​(xn)​F​(φ)\frac{\delta^{n}}{\varphi(x_{1})\dots\varphi(x_{n})}F(\varphi)=f(x_{1})\dots f(x_{n})F(\varphi) (58)

and hence

(F⋆G)​(φ)\displaystyle(F\star G)(\varphi) (59)
=∑n=0∞1n!​(∫d​x​𝑑y​i​ℏ2​ΔS​(x,y)​f​(x)​g​(y))n​F​(φ)​G​(φ)\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\left(\int dxdy\frac{i\hbar}{2}\Delta_{S}(x,y)f(x)g(y)\right)^{n}\,F(\varphi)G(\varphi) (60)

For later purposes we want to extend the product to more singular functionals which includes in particular the local functionals. We split

i2​ΔS=ΔS+−ΔS−\tfrac{i}{2}\Delta_{S}=\Delta_{S}^{+}-\Delta_{S}^{-} (61)

in such a way that the wavefront set of ΔS\Delta_{S} is decomposed into two disjoint parts. The wave front set of ΔS\Delta_{S} consists of pairs of points x,x′x,x^{\prime} which can be connected by a null geodesic, and of covectors (k,k′)(k,k^{\prime}) where kk is the cotangent vector of the null geodesic at xx and −k′-k^{\prime} is the cotangent vector of the same null geodesic at x′x^{\prime}. The lightcone with the origin removed consists of two disjoint components, the first one containing the positive frequencies and the other one the negative frequencies. The WF set of the positive frequency part of ΔS\Delta_{S} is therefore:

WF(ΔS+)={(x,k;x′,−k′)∈T˙M2|(x,k)∼(x′,k′),k∈(V¯+)x}.\mathrm{WF}(\Delta_{S}^{+})=\{(x,k;x′,-k^{\prime})\in\dot{T}M^{2}|(x,k)\sim(x^{\prime},k^{\prime}),k\in(\overline{V}_{+})_{x}\}\,. (62)

On Minkowski space one could choose ΔS+\Delta_{S}^{+} as the Wightman 2-point-function, i.e. the vacuum expectation value of the product of two fields. This, however, becomes meaningless in a more general context, since a generally covariant concept of a vacuum state does not exist. Nevertheless, such a decomposition always exist, but is not unique and the difference between two different choices of ΔS+\Delta_{S}^{+} is always a smooth symmetric function. Let us write ΔS+=i2​ΔS+H\Delta_{S}^{+}=\tfrac{i}{2}\Delta_{S}+H We then consider the linear functional derivative operator

ΓH=⟨H,δ2δ​φ2⟩\Gamma_{H}=\langle H,\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta\varphi^{2}}\rangle (63)

and define a new ⋆\star-product by

F⋆HG=αH​((αH−1​F)⋆(αH−1​G)),F\star_{H}G=\alpha_{H}\left((\alpha^{-1}_{H}F)\star(\alpha_{H}^{-1}G)\right)\,, (64)

where αH≐eℏ2​ΓH\alpha_{H}\doteq e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}\Gamma_{H}}. This product differs from the original one in the replacement of i2​ΔS\frac{i}{2}\Delta_{S} by ΔS+\Delta_{S}^{+}. This star product can now be defined on a much larger space of functionals, namely the microcausal ones 𝔉μ​c​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M). The transition between these two star products correspond to normal ordering, and the ⋆H\star_{H}-product is just an algebraic version of Wick’s theorem. The map αH\alpha_{H} provides the equivalence between ⋆\star and ⋆H\star_{H} on the space of regular functionals 𝔉reg​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{reg}}(M). Its image can be then completed to a larger space 𝔉μ​c​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M). We can also build a corresponding (sequential) completion αH−1​(𝔉μ​c​(M))\alpha_{H}^{-1}(\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M)) of the source space. This amounts to extending 𝔉reg​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{reg}}(M) with all elements of the form limn→∞αH−1​(Fn)\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\alpha_{H}^{-1}(F_{n}), where (Fn)(F_{n}) is a convergent sequence in 𝔉μ​c​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M) with respect to the Hörmander topology [12, 35]. We recall now the definition of this topology.

Definition 5.1.

Let us denote the space of compactly supported distributions with WF sets contained in a conical set C⊂T∗​MnC\subset T^{*}M^{n} by ℰC′​(Mn)\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{C}(M^{n}). Now let Cn⊂ΞnC_{n}\subset\Xi_{n} be a closed cone contained in Ξn\Xi_{n} defined by (53). We introduce (after [35, 1, 12]) the following family of seminorms on ℰCn′​(Mn)\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{C_{n}}(M^{n}):

pn,φ,C~,k​(u)=supk∈C~{(1+|k|)k​|φ​u^​(k)|},p_{n,\varphi,\tilde{C},k}(u)=\sup_{{k}\in\tilde{C}}\{(1+|{k}|)^{k}|\widehat{\varphi u}({k})|\}\,,

where the index set consists of (n,φ,C~,k)(n,\varphi,\tilde{C},k) such that k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, φ∈𝒟⁡(M)\varphi\in\mathcal{D}(M) and C~\tilde{C} is a closed cone in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with (supp⁡(φ)×C~)∩Cn=∅(\mathrm{supp}(\varphi)\times\tilde{C})\cap C_{n}=\varnothing. These seminorms, together with the seminorms of the weak topology provide a defining system for a locally convex topology denoted by τCn\tau_{C_{n}}. To control the wave front set properties inside open cones, we take an inductive limit. The resulting topology is denoted by τΞn\tau_{\Xi_{n}}. One can show that 𝒟⁡(M)\mathcal{D}(M) is sequentially dense in ℰΞn′​(M)\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{\Xi_{n}}(M) in this topology.

For microcausal functionals it holds that F(n)​(φ)∈ℰΞn′​(M)F^{(n)}(\varphi)\in\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{\Xi_{n}}(M), so we can equip 𝔉μ​c​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M) with the initial topology with respect to mappings:

𝒞∞​(𝔈⁡(M),ℝ)∋F↦F(n)​(φ)∈(ℰΞn​(M),τΞn)n≥0,\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathfrak{E}(M),\mathbb{R})\ni F\mapsto F^{(n)}(\varphi)\in(\mathcal{E}_{\Xi_{n}}(M),\tau_{\Xi_{n}})\quad n\geq 0\,, (65)

and denote this topology by τΞ\tau_{\Xi}.

The locally convex vector space of local functionals 𝔉loc​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M) is dense in 𝔉μ​c​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M) with respect to τΞ\tau_{\Xi}. To see these abstract concepts at work let us consider the example of the Wick square:

Example 5.2.

Consider a sequence Fn​(φ)=∫φ⁡(x)​φ​(y)​gn​(y−x)​f​(x)F_{n}(\varphi)=\int\varphi(x)\varphi(y)g_{n}(y-x)f(x) with a smooth function ff and a sequence of smooth functions gng_{n} which converges to the δ\delta distribution in the Hörmander topology. By applying αH−1=e−ℏ2​ΓH\alpha_{H}^{-1}=e^{-\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\Gamma_{H}}, we obtain a sequence

αH−1​Fn=∫(φ⁡(x)​φ​(y)​gn​(y−x)​f​(x)−H⁡(x,y)​gn​(y−x)​f​(x)),\alpha_{H}^{-1}F_{n}=\int(\varphi(x)\varphi(y)g_{n}(y-x)f(x)-H(x,y)g_{n}(y-x)f(x))\,,

The limit of this sequence can be identified with ∫:φ​(x)2:f⁡(x)\int:\varphi(x)^{2}:f(x), i.e.:

∫:φ​(x)2:f⁡(x)=limn→∞∫(φ⁡(x)​φ​(y)−H⁡(x,y))​gn​(y−x)​f​(x)\int:\varphi(x)^{2}:f(x)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\int(\varphi(x)\varphi(y)-H(x,y))g_{n}(y-x)f(x)

We can write it in a short-hand notation as a coinciding point limit:

:φ​(x)2:=limy→x(φ⁡(x)​φ​(y)−H⁡(x,y)).:\varphi(x)^{2}:\,=\lim_{y\rightarrow x}(\varphi(x)\varphi(y)-H(x,y))\,.

We can see that transforming with αH−1\alpha_{H}^{-1} corresponds formally to a subtraction of H⁡(x,y)H(x,y). Now, to recognize the Wick’s theorem let us consider a product of two Wick squares :φ​(x)2::φ​(y)2::\varphi(x)^{2}::\varphi(y)^{2}:. With the use of the isomorphism αH−1\alpha_{H}^{-1} this can be written as:

∫φ​(x)2​f1​(x)⋆∫H⁡φ​(y)2​f2​(y)=∫φ​(x)2​φ​(y)2​f1​(x)​f2​(y)+2​i​ℏ​∫φ⁡(x)​φ​(y)​ΔS+​(x,y)​f1​(x)​f2​(y)−ℏ2​∫(ΔS+​(x,y))2​f1​(x)​f2​(y).\int\varphi(x)^{2}f_{1}(x)\star_{H}\int\varphi(y)^{2}f_{2}(y)=\\ \int\varphi(x)^{2}\varphi(y)^{2}f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y)+2i\hbar\int\varphi(x)\varphi(y)\Delta_{S}^{+}(x,y)f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y)-\hbar^{2}\int(\Delta_{S}^{+}(x,y))^{2}f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y)\,.

Omitting the test functions and using αH−1\alpha_{H}^{-1} we obtain

:φ​(x)2::φ​(y)2:=:φ​(x)2​φ​(y)2:+4:φ⁡(x)​φ​(y):i​ℏ2​ΔS+​(x,y)+2​(i​ℏ2​ΔS+​(x,y))2,:\varphi(x)^{2}::\varphi(y)^{2}:=:\varphi(x)^{2}\varphi(y)^{2}:+4:\varphi(x)\varphi(y):\frac{i\hbar}{2}\Delta_{S}^{+}(x,y)+2\Big(\frac{i\hbar}{2}\Delta_{S}^{+}(x,y)\Big)^{2}\,,

which is a familiar form of the Wick’s theorem applied to :φ​(x)2::φ​(y)2::\varphi(x)^{2}::\varphi(y)^{2}:.

Different choices of HH differ only by a smooth function, hence all the algebras (αH−1​(𝔉μ​c​(M)​[[ℏ]]),⋆)(\alpha_{H}^{-1}(\mathfrak{F}_{\mu\mathrm{c}}(M)[[\hbar]]),\star) are isomorphic and define an abstract algebra 𝔄⁡(M)\mathfrak{A}(M). Since for F∈𝔄⁡(M)F\in\mathfrak{A}(M) it holds αHF∈𝔄H(M)=(𝔉μ​c(M)[[ℏ]],⋆H)\alpha_{H}F\in\mathfrak{A}_{H}(M)=(\mathfrak{F}_{{\mu\mathrm{c}}}(M)[[\hbar]],\star_{H}), we can realize 𝔄⁡(M)\mathfrak{A}(M) more concretely as the space of families {αH​F}H\{\alpha_{H}F\}_{H}, numbered by possible choices of HH, where F∈𝔄⁡(M)F\in\mathfrak{A}(M), fulfilling the relation

FH′=exp⁡(ℏ​ΓH′−H)​FH,F_{H^{\prime}}=\exp(\hbar\Gamma_{H^{\prime}-H})F_{H}\,,

equipped with the product

(F⋆G)H=FH⋆HGH.(F\star G)_{H}=F_{H}\star_{H}G_{H}.

The support of F∈𝔄⁡(M)F\in\mathfrak{A}(M) is defined as supp⁡(F)=supp⁡(αH​F)\mathrm{supp}(F)=\mathrm{supp}(\alpha_{H}F). Again, this is indepedent of HH. Functional derivatives are defined by

⟨δ​Fδ​φ,ψ⟩=αH−1​⟨δ​αH​Fδ​φ,ψ⟩,\left<\frac{\delta F}{\delta\varphi},\psi\right>=\alpha_{H}^{-1}\left<\frac{\delta\alpha_{H}F}{\delta\varphi},\psi\right>\,,

which is well defined as ΓH′−H\Gamma_{H^{\prime}-H} commutes with functional derivatives. In the next step we want to define the involution on our algebra. Note that the complex conjugation satisfies the relation:

F⋆G¯=G¯⋆F¯.\overline{F\star G}=\overline{G}\star\overline{F}\,. (66)

Therefore we can use it to define an involution F∗​(φ)≐F⁡(φ)¯F^{*}(\varphi)\doteq\overline{F(\varphi)}. The resulting structure is an involutive noncommutative algebra 𝔄⁡(M)\mathfrak{A}(M), which provides a quantization of (𝔉μ​c(M),{.,.}S)(\mathfrak{F}_{{\mu\mathrm{c}}}(M),\{.,.\}_{S}). To see that this is equivalent to canonical quantization, let us look at the commutator of two smeared fields Φ⁡(f)\Phi(f), Φ⁡(g)\Phi(g), where Φ⁡(f)​(φ)≐∫f​φ​dvolM\Phi(f)(\varphi)\doteq\int\!f\varphi\,\ \mathrm{dvol}_{\scriptscriptstyle{M}}. The commutator reads

[Φ(f),Φ(g)]⋆H=iℏ⟨f,ΔSg⟩,f,g∈𝔇(M),[\Phi(f),\Phi(g)]_{\star_{H}}=i\hbar\langle f,\Delta_{S}g\rangle\ ,\quad f,g\in\mathfrak{D}(M)\,,

This indeed reproduces the canonical commutation relations. Here we used the fact that the choice of ΔS+\Delta_{S}^{+} is unique up to a symmetric function, which doesn’t contribute to the commutator (which is antisymmetric). In case ΔS+\Delta_{S}^{+} is a distribution of positive type (as in the case of the Wightman 2-point-function) the linear functional on 𝔉⁡(M)\mathfrak{F}(M)

ω⁡(F)=F⁡(0)\omega(F)=F(0) (67)

is a state (the vacuum state in the special case above), and the associated GNS representation is the Fock representation. The kernel of the representation is the ideal generated by the field equation.

Let us now discuss the covariance properties of Wick products. As seen in example 5.2, polynomial functionals in 𝔄H​(ℳ)\mathfrak{A}_{H}(\mathcal{M}) can be interpreted as Wick polynomials. Corresponding elements of 𝔄⁡(ℳ)\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{M}) can be obtained by applying αH−1\alpha_{H}^{-1}. The resulting object will be denoted by

∫:Φx1…Φxn:Hf(x1,…,xn)≐αH−1(∫Φx1…Φxnf(x1,…,xn)).\int:\Phi_{x_{1}}\dots\Phi_{x_{n}}:_{H}f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\doteq\alpha^{-1}_{H}\Big(\int\Phi_{x_{1}}\dots\Phi_{x_{n}}f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\Big)\,. (68)

where Φxi\Phi_{x_{i}} are evaluation functionals, f∈ℰΞn′​(Mn,V)f\in\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{\Xi_{n}}(M^{n},V).

The assignment of 𝔄⁡(M)\mathfrak{A}(M) to a spacetime MM can be made into a functor 𝔄\mathfrak{A} from the category 𝐋𝐨𝐜\mathrm{\mathbf{Loc}} of spacetimes to the category of topological *-algebras 𝐎𝐛𝐬\mathrm{\mathbf{Obs}} and by composing with a forgetful functor to the category 𝐕𝐞𝐜\mathrm{\mathbf{Vec}} of topological vector spaces. Admissible embeddings are mapped to pullbacks, i.e. for χ:M→M′\chi:M\rightarrow M^{\prime} we set 𝔄​χ​F​(φ)≐F⁡(χ∗​φ)\mathfrak{A}\chi F(\varphi)\doteq F(\chi^{*}\varphi). Locally covariant quantum fields are natural transformations between 𝔇\mathfrak{D} and 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. Let us denote the extended space of locally covariant quantum fields by ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q}. We shall require Wick powers to be elements of ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q} in the above sense. On each object MM we have to construct the map 𝒯1M{\mathcal{T}_{1}}_{M} from the classical algebra 𝔉loc​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M) to the quantum algebra 𝔄⁡(M)\mathfrak{A}(M) in such a way that

𝒯1M​(ΦM​(f))​(χ∗​φ)=𝒯1M′​(ΦM′​(χ∗​f))​(φ).{\mathcal{T}_{1}}_{M}(\Phi_{M}(f))(\chi^{*}\varphi)={\mathcal{T}_{1}}_{M^{\prime}}(\Phi_{M^{\prime}}(\chi_{*}f))(\varphi)\,. (69)

As we noted above, classical functionals can be mapped to 𝔄H​(M)\mathfrak{A}_{H}(M) by identification (68). This however doesn’t have right covariance properties. A detailed discussion is presented in section 5 of [11]. Here we only give a a sketch of the argument for the Wick square. For each object M∈𝐋𝐨𝐜M\in\mathrm{\mathbf{Loc}} we choose HMH_{M} (so 𝒯1M=αHM−1{\mathcal{T}_{1}}_{M}=\alpha^{-1}_{H_{M}} ) and going through the definitions it is easy to see that, for an admissible embedding χ:M→M′\chi:M\rightarrow M^{\prime}

𝔄χ(:Φ2:HM(x))=:Φ2:HM′(χ(x))+HM′(χ(x),(x))−HM(x,x)\mathfrak{A}\chi\big(:\Phi^{2}:_{H_{M}}(x)\big)=:\Phi^{2}:_{H_{M^{\prime}}}(\chi(x))+H_{M^{\prime}}(\chi(x),(x))-H_{M}(x,x)

holds. It was shown in [11] that redefining Wick powers to become covariant amounts to solving certain cohomological problem. The result reproduces the solution, proposed earlier in [31], to define 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} as αH+w−1\alpha^{-1}_{H+w}, where ww is the smooth part of the Hadamard 2-point function ω=uσ+v​ln⁡σ+w\omega=\frac{u}{\sigma}+v\ln\sigma+w with σ⁡(x,y)\sigma(x,y) denoting the square of the length of the geodesic connecting xx and yy and with geometrical determined smooth functions uu and vv.

6 Interacting theories and the time ordered product

If we have an action for which SM′′S^{\prime\prime}_{M} still depends on φ\varphi, we choose a particular φ0\varphi_{0} and split

SM​(φ0+ψ)=12​⟨SM′′​(φ0),ψ⊗ψ⟩+SI​(φ0,ψ).S_{M}(\varphi_{0}+\psi)=\frac{1}{2}\langle S_{M}^{\prime\prime}(\varphi_{0}),\psi\otimes\psi\rangle+S_{I}(\varphi_{0},\psi)\ . (70)

From now on we drop the subscript MM of SIS_{I}, since it’s clear that we work on a fixed manifold. We now introduce the linear operator

𝒯=ei​ℏ​⟨ΔSD,δ2δ​ψ2⟩\mathcal{T}=e^{i\hbar\langle\Delta_{S}^{D},\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta\psi^{2}}\rangle} (71)

which acts on 𝔉reg​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{\mathrm{reg}}(M) as

(𝒯​F)​(φ)≐∑n=0∞ℏnn!​⟨(i​ΔSD)⊗n,F(2​n)​(φ)⟩,,(\mathcal{T}F)(\varphi)\doteq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\hbar^{n}}{n!}\left<(i\Delta_{S}^{D})^{\otimes n},F^{(2n)}(\varphi)\right>,\,,

with the Dirac propagator ΔSD=12​(ΔSR+ΔSA)\Delta_{S}^{D}=\frac{1}{2}(\Delta_{S}^{R}+\Delta_{S}^{A}) at φ0\varphi_{0}. Formally, 𝒯\mathcal{T} may be understood as the operator of convolution with the oscillating Gaussian measure with covariance i​ℏ​ΔSDi\hbar\Delta_{S}^{D}. By

F⋅𝒯G=𝒯(𝒯−1F⋅𝒯−1G)F\cdot_{{}^{\mathcal{T}}}G=\mathcal{T}\left(\mathcal{T}^{-1}F\cdot\mathcal{T}^{-1}G\right) (72)

we define a new product on 𝔉⁡(M)\mathfrak{F}(M) which is the time ordered product with respect to ⋆\star and which is equivalent to the pointwise product of classical field theory. We then define a linear map

RSIF=(e𝒯SI)⋆−1⋆(e𝒯SI⋅𝒯F)R_{S_{I}}F=\Big(e_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{T}}}^{S_{I}}\Big)^{\star-1}\star\left(e_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{T}}}^{S_{I}}\cdot_{{}^{\mathcal{T}}}F\right) (73)

where e𝒯e_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{T}}} is the exponential function with respect to the time ordered product,

e𝒯F=𝒯⁡(e𝒯−1​F).e_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{T}}}^{F}=\mathcal{T}\big(e^{\mathcal{T}^{-1}F}\big)\ . (74)

RSIR_{S_{I}} is invertible with the inverse

RSI−1​F=eT−SI⋅T(eTSI⋆F)R_{S_{I}}^{-1}F=e_{T}^{-S_{I}}\cdot_{T}\left(e_{T}^{S_{I}}\star F\right) (75)

We now define the ⋆\star product for the full action by

F⋆SG=RSI−1​(RSI​F⋆RSI​G)F\star_{S}G=R_{S_{I}}^{-1}\left(R_{S_{I}}F\star R_{S_{I}}G\right) (76)

7 Renormalization

Unfortunately, the algebraic structures discussed so far are well defined only if SIS_{I} is a regular functional. An easy extension is provided by the operation of normal ordering as described in the section of deformation quantization. This operation transforms the time ordering operator 𝒯\mathcal{T} into another one 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime}, such that the new time ordered product is now defined with respect to the Feynman propagator ΔSF=i​ΔSD+H\Delta_{S}^{F}=i\Delta_{S}^{D}+H, no longer the Dirac propagator ΔSD\Delta_{S}^{D}. Note that the Feynman propagator does depend on the choice of ΔS+\Delta_{S}^{+}. Contrary to the ⋆H\star_{H} product which is everywhere defined due to the wave front set properties of the positive frequency part of ΔS\Delta_{S} the time ordered product is in general undefined since the wave front set of the Feynman propagator contains the wave front set of the δ\delta-function. We want, however, to extend to a larger class which contains in particular all local functionals. As already proposed by Stückelberg [52] and Bogoliubov [3, 4] and carefully worked out by Epstein and Glaser [22], the crucial problem is the definition of time ordered products of local functionals. Let us first consider a special case.

Let F=12​∫d​x​φ​(x)2​f​(x)F=\frac{1}{2}\int dx\varphi(x)^{2}f(x), G=12​∫d​x​φ​(x)2​g​(x)G=\frac{1}{2}\int dx\varphi(x)^{2}g(x). Then the time ordered product ⋅𝒯′\cdot_{\mathcal{T}^{\prime}} is formally given by

(F⋅𝒯′G)​(φ)=F⁡(φ)​G​(φ)+i​ℏ​∫d​x​𝑑y​φ​(x)​φ​(y)​f​(x)​g​(y)​ΔSF​(x,y)−ℏ22​∫d​x​𝑑y​ΔSF​(x,y)2​f​(x)​g​(y).(F\cdot_{\mathcal{T}^{\prime}}G)(\varphi)=F(\varphi)G(\varphi)+i\hbar\int dxdy\varphi(x)\varphi(y)f(x)g(y)\Delta_{S}^{F}(x,y)-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2}\int dxdy\Delta_{S}^{F}(x,y)^{2}f(x)g(y)\ . (77)

But the last term contains the pointwise product of a distribution with itself. For x≠yx\not=y the covectors (k,k′)(k,k^{\prime}) in the wave front set satisfy the condition that kk and −k′-k^{\prime} are cotangent to an (affinely parametrized) null geodesics connecting xx and yy. kk is future directed if xx is in the future of yy and past directed otherwise. Hence the sum of two such covectors cannot vanish. Therefore the theorem on the multiplicability of distributions applies and yields a distribution on the complement of the diagonal {(x,x)|x∈M}\{(x,x)|x\in M\}. On the diagonal, however, the only restriction is k=−k′k=-k^{\prime}, hence the sum of the wave front set of ΔSF\Delta_{S}^{F} with itself meets the zero section of the cotangent bundle at the diagonal.

In general the time-ordered product 𝒯n(F1,…,Fn)≐F1⋅𝒯⋯⋅𝒯Fn\mathcal{T}_{n}(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n})\doteq F_{1}\cdot_{{}^{\mathcal{T}}}\dots\cdot_{{}^{\mathcal{T}}}F_{n} of nn local functionals is well defined for local entries as long as supports of F1,…,FnF_{1},\ldots,F_{n} are pairwise disjoint. The technical problem one now has to solve is the extension of a distribution which is defined outside of a submanifold to an everywhere defined distribution. In the case of QFT on Minkowski space one can exploit translation invariance and reduce the problem in the relative coordinates to the extension problem of a distribution defined outside of the origin in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. The crucial concept for this extension problem is Steinmann’s scaling degree [53].

Definition 7.1.

Let U⊂ℝnU\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a scale invariant open subset (i.e. λ​U=U\lambda U=U for λ>0\lambda>0), and let t∈𝒟′​(U)t\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U) be a distribution on UU. Let tλ​(x)=t⁡(λ​x)t_{\lambda}(x)=t(\lambda x) be the scaled distribution. The scaling degree sd\mathrm{sd} of tt is

sd​t=inf⁡{δ∈ℝ|limλ→0λδ​tλ=0}.\mathrm{sd}\,t=\mathrm{inf}\{\delta\in\mathbb{R}|\lim_{\lambda\to 0}\lambda^{\delta}t_{\lambda}=0\}\ . (78)

There is one more important concept related to the scaling degree, namely the degree of divergence. It is defined as:

div⁡(t)≐sd⁡(t)−n.\mathrm{div}(t)\doteq\mathrm{sd}(t)-n\,.
Theorem 7.2.

Let t∈𝒟⁡(ℝn∖{0})t\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}) with scaling degree sd​t<∞\mathrm{sd}\,t<\infty. Then there exists an extension of tt to an everywhere defined distribution with the same scaling degree. The extension is unique up to the addition of a derivative P⁡(∂)​δP(\partial)\delta of the delta function, where PP is a polynomial with degree bounded by div⁡(t)\mathrm{div}(t) (hence vanishes for sd​t<n\mathrm{sd}\,t<n).

A proof may be found in [19]. In the example above the scaling degree of ΔSF​(x)2\Delta_{S}^{F}(x)^{2} is 4 (in 4 dimensions). Hence the extension exists and is unique up to the addition of a multiple of the delta function.

The theorem above replaces the cumbersome estimates on conditional convergence of Feynman integrals on Minkowski momentum space. Often this convergence is not proven at all, instead the convergence of the corresponding integrals on momentum space with euclidean signature is shown. The transition to Minkowski signature is then made after the integration. This amounts not to a computation but merely to a definition of the originally undefined Minkowski space integral.

The generalization of the theorem on the extension of distributions to the situation met on curved spacetimes is due to Brunetti and one of us (K.F.) [7]. It uses techniques of microlocal analysis to reduce the general situation to the case covered by the theorem above.

The construction of time ordered products is then performed in the following way (causal perturbation theory). One searches for a family (𝒯n)n∈ℕ0(\mathcal{T}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}} of nn-linear symmetric maps from local functionals to microcausal functionals subject to the following conditions:

  1. T 1.

    𝒯0=1\mathcal{T}_{0}=1,

  2. T 2.

    𝒯1=id\mathcal{T}_{1}=\mathrm{id} (for curved spacetime one should rather choose 𝒯1=eΓw\mathcal{T}_{1}=e^{\Gamma_{w}}, see the discussion at the end of the section 5),

  3. T 3.

    𝒯n​(F1,…,Fn)=𝒯k​(F1,…,Fk)⋆𝒯n−k​(Fk+1,…,Fn)\mathcal{T}_{n}(F_{1},\dots,F_{n})=\mathcal{T}_{k}(F_{1},\dots,F_{k})\star\mathcal{T}_{n-k}(F_{k+1},\dots,F_{n}) if the supports supp​Fi\mathrm{supp}F_{i}, i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k of the first kk entries do not intersect the past of the supports supp​Fj\mathrm{supp}F_{j}, j=k+1,…,nj=k+1,\dots,n of the last n−kn-k entries (causal factorisation property).

The construction proceeds by induction: when the first nn maps 𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k}, k=0,…,nk=0,\dots,n have been determined, the map 𝒯n+1\mathcal{T}_{n+1} is determined up to an (n+1)(n+1)-linear map Zn+1Z_{n+1} from local functionals to local functionals. This ambiguity corresponds directly to the freedom of adding finite counterterms in every order in perturbation theory.

The general result can be conveniently formulated in terms of the formal S-matrix, defined as the generating function of time ordered products,

𝒮⁡(V)=∑n=0∞1n!​𝒯n​(V,…,V).\mathcal{S}(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\mathcal{T}_{n}(V,\dots,V)\ . (79)

Then the S-matrix 𝒮^\hat{\mathcal{S}} with respect to an other sequence of time ordered products is related to 𝒮\mathcal{S} by

𝒮^=𝒮∘Z\hat{\mathcal{S}}=\mathcal{S}\circ Z (80)

where ZZ maps local functionals to local functionals, is analytic with vanishing zero order term and with the first order term being the identity. The maps ZZ form the renormalization group in the sense of Petermann and Stückelberg. They are formal diffeomorphisms on the space of local functionals and describe the allowed finite renormalization.

In order to illustrate the methods described above we work out the combinatorics in terms of Feynman diagrams (graphs). Let DD be the second order functional differential operator D=i​ℏ2​⟨ΔSF,δ2δ​φ2⟩D=\frac{i\hbar}{2}\langle\Delta_{S}^{F},\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta\varphi^{2}}\rangle. The time ordered product of nn factors is formally given by

F1⋅𝒯…​Fn≡𝒯n​(F1,…​Fn)=e12​D​(e−12​D​F1⋅…​e−12​D​Fn)F_{1}\cdot_{\mathcal{T}}\dots F_{n}\equiv\mathcal{T}_{n}(F_{1},\dots F_{n})=e^{\frac{1}{2}D}(e^{-\frac{1}{2}D}F_{1}\cdot\dots e^{-\frac{1}{2}D}F_{n})

Using Leibniz’ rule and the fact that DD is of second order we find

(F1⋅𝒯…Fn)(φ)=e∑i<jDi​jF1(φ1)⋯Fn(φn)|φ1=…​φn=φ(F_{1}\cdot_{\mathcal{T}}\dots F_{n})(\varphi)=e^{\sum_{i<j}D_{ij}}F_{1}(\varphi_{1})\cdots F_{n}(\varphi_{n})|_{\varphi_{1}=\dots\varphi_{n}=\varphi} (81)

with Di​j=i​ℏ​⟨ΔSF,δ2δ​φi​δ​φj⟩D_{ij}=i\hbar\langle\Delta_{S}^{F},\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta\varphi_{i}\delta\varphi_{j}}\rangle. The expansion of the exponential function of the differential operator yields

𝒯n=∑Γ∈Gn𝒯Γ\mathcal{T}_{n}=\sum_{\Gamma\in G_{n}}\mathcal{T}_{\Gamma} (83)

with GnG_{n} the set of all graphs with vertices {1,…​n}\{1,\dots n\} and 𝒯Γ=1Sym​(Γ)​⟨S~Γ,δΓ⟩\mathcal{T}_{\Gamma}=\frac{1}{\textrm{Sym}(\Gamma)}\langle\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma},\delta_{\Gamma}\rangle where

and the symmetry factor is Sym​(Γ)=∏i<jli​j!\textrm{Sym}(\Gamma)=\prod_{i<j}l_{ij}!. Note that S~Γ\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma} is a well-defined distribution in 𝒟′​((𝕄2\Diag)|E⁡(Γ)|)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}((\mathbb{M}^{2}\backslash\mathrm{Diag})^{\left|E(\Gamma)\right|}) (Diag\mathrm{Diag} denotes the thin diagonal) that can be uniquely extended to 𝒟′​(𝕄2​|E⁡(Γ)|)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}^{2\left|E(\Gamma)\right|}), since the Feynman fundamental solution has a unique extension with the same scaling degree. More explicitly we can write (83) as:

𝒯n​(F1,…,Fn)=∑Γ∈Gn1Sym​(Γ)​⟨S~Γ,δΓ​(F1,…,Fn)⟩\mathcal{T}_{n}(F_{1},\dots,F_{n})=\sum_{\Gamma\in G_{n}}\frac{1}{\textrm{Sym}(\Gamma)}\langle\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma},\delta_{\Gamma}(F_{1},\dots,F_{n})\rangle (84)

Graphically we represent FF with a vertex ††feynman-diagram: (Feynman diagram, (x5) and Di​jD_{ij} with a dumbbell i††feynman-diagram: (Feynman diagram, (x2)j{}_{i}\parbox{28.45274pt}{\begin{center}\begin{fmfgraph}{2}0,10) \end{fmfgraph}\end{center}}{}_{j}, so each empty circle corresponds to a functional derivative. Applying the derivative on a functional can be pictorially represented as filling the circle with the vertex. Note that the expansion in graphs is possible due to the fact that the action used as a starting point is quadratic, so DD is a second order differential operator. If it were of order k>2k>2, instead of lines we would have had to use k−1k-1 simplices to represent it. Let us illustrate the concepts which we introduced here on a simple example.

Example 7.3 (removing tadpoles).

Let us look at the definition of the time ordered product of FF and GG in low orders in ℏ\hbar. We can write D⁡(F⋅G)D(F\cdot G) diagramatically as:
