All the loop terms cancel out. We can see that applying e−12​De^{-\frac{1}{2}D} on GG and FF reflects what is called in physics “removing the tadpoles”. In formula (82) it is reflected by the fact that we set li​i=0l_{ii}=0.

As long as the formula (81) is applied to regular functionals there is no problem, since their functional derivatives are by definition test functions. But the relevant functionals are the interaction Lagrangians which are local functionals and therefore have derivatives with support on the thin diagonal, hence all but the first derivative are singular. As a typical example consider

F⁡(φ)=∫d​z​f​(z)​φ​(z)kk!.F(\varphi)=\int dzf(z)\frac{\varphi(z)^{k}}{k!}\ .

Its derivatives are

F(l)​[φ]​(x1,…,xl)=∫d​z​f​(z)​φ​(z)k−l(k−l)!​∏iδ⁡(z−xi).F^{(l)}[\varphi](x_{1},\dots,x_{l})=\int dzf(z)\frac{\varphi(z)^{k-l}}{(k-l)!}\prod_{i}\delta(z-x_{i})\ . (86)

In general, the functional derivatives of a local functional have the form

F(l)[φ](x1,…,xl)=∫dz∑jfj[φ](z)pj(∂x1,…,∂xl)∏i=1lδ(z−xi)F^{(l)}[\varphi](x_{1},\dots,x_{l})=\int dz\sum_{j}f_{j}[\varphi](z)p_{j}(\partial_{x_{1}},\dots,\partial_{x_{l}})\prod_{i=1}^{l}\delta(z-x_{i})

with polynomials pjp_{j} and φ\varphi-dependent test functions fj​[φ]f_{j}[\varphi]. The integral representation above is not unique since one can add total derivatives. This amounts to the relation

∫dzq(∂z)f(z)p(∂x1,…,∂xl)∏iδ(z−xi)=∫dzf(z)q(∂x1+…∂xl)p(∂x1,…,∂xl)∏iδ(z−xi).\int dzq(\partial_{z})f(z)p(\partial_{x_{1}},\dots,\partial_{x_{l}})\prod_{i}\delta(z-x_{i})=\int dzf(z)q(\partial_{x_{1}}+\dots\partial_{x_{l}})p(\partial_{x_{1}},\dots,\partial_{x_{l}})\prod_{i}\delta(z-x_{i})\ . (87)

We insert the integral representation (86) into the formula (84) for the time ordered product and in each term we obtain:

⟨S~Γ,δΓ(F1,…,Fn)⟩=∫dx→dz→∏v∈V⁡(Γ)(∑jvfjvv[φ](zv)pjv(∂xe,v|v∈∂e)∏e:v∈∂eαvδ4(zv−xe,v))S~Γ,\langle\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma},\delta_{\Gamma}(F_{1},\dots,F_{n})\rangle=\int\!\!d\vec{x}d\vec{z}\prod\limits_{v\in V(\Gamma)}\Big(\sum\limits_{j_{v}}f^{v}_{j_{v}}[\varphi](z_{v})p_{j_{v}}(\partial_{x_{e,v}}|v\in\partial e)\prod\limits_{\mathclap{e:v\in\partial e}}^{\alpha_{v}}\delta^{4}(z_{v}-x_{e,v})\Big)\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma}\,,

where αv\alpha_{v} is the number of lines adjacent at vertex vv and we use the notation x→=(xe,v|e∈E⁡(Γ),v∈∂e)\vec{x}=(x_{e,v}|e\in E(\Gamma),v\in\partial e), z→=(zv|v∈V⁡(Γ))\vec{z}=(z_{v}|v\in V(\Gamma)). We can move the partial derivatives ∂xe,v\partial_{x_{e,v}} by formal partial integration to the distribution S~Γ\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma}. Next we integrate over the delta distributions, which amounts to the pullback of a derivative of S~Γ\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma} with respect to the map ρΓ:𝕄|V⁡(Γ)|→𝕄2​|E⁡(Γ)|\rho_{\Gamma}:\mathbb{M}^{|V(\Gamma)|}\rightarrow\mathbb{M}^{2|E(\Gamma)|} given by the prescription

(ρΓ​(z))e,v=zvif​v∈∂e.(\rho_{\Gamma}(z))_{e,v}=z_{v}\,\quad\mathrm{if}\,v\in\partial e\,.

Let pp be a polynomial in the derivatives with respect to the partial derivatives ∂xe,v,v∈∂e\partial_{x_{e,v}},v\in\partial e. The pullback ρΓ∗\rho_{\Gamma}^{*} of p​S~Γp\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma} is well defined on 𝕄|V⁡(Γ)|\DIAG\mathbb{M}^{\left|V(\Gamma)\right|}\backslash\mathrm{DIAG}, where DIAG\mathrm{DIAG} is the large diagonal:

DIAG={z∈𝕄|V⁡(Γ)||∃v,w∈V(Γ),v≠w:zv=zw}.\mathrm{DIAG}=\left\{z\in\mathbb{M}^{\left|V(\Gamma)\right|}|\,\exists v,w\in V(\Gamma),v\neq w:\,z_{v}=z_{w}\right\}\,.

The problem of renormalization now amounts to finding the extensions of ρΓ∗​p​S~Γ\rho_{\Gamma}^{*}p\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma} to everywhere defined distributions SΓ,p∈𝒟′​(𝕄|V⁡(Γ)|)S_{\Gamma,p}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}^{\left|V(\Gamma)\right|}) which depend linearly on pp. These extensions must satisfy the relation

∂zvSΓ,p=SΓ,(∑e∂xe,v)p\partial_{z_{v}}S_{\Gamma,p}=S_{\Gamma,(\sum_{e}\partial_{x_{e,v}})p} (88)

We present now the inductive procedure of Epstein and Glaser that allows to define the desired extension of ρΓ∗​p​S~Γ\rho_{\Gamma}^{*}p\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma}. For the simplicity of notation we first consider the case where no derivative couplings are present.

Let us define an Epstein-Glaser subgraph (EG subgraph) γ⊆Γ\gamma\subseteq\Gamma to be a subset of the set of vertices V⁡(γ)⊆V⁡(Γ)V(\gamma)\subseteq V(\Gamma) together with all lines in Γ\Gamma connecting them,

E⁡(γ)={e∈E⁡(Γ):∂e⊂V⁡(γ)}.E(\gamma)=\left\{e\in E(\Gamma):\partial e\subset V(\gamma)\right\}.

The first step of the Epstein-Glaser induction is to choose extensions for all EG subgraphs with two vertices, |V⁡(γ)|=2\left|V(\gamma)\right|=2. In this case we have translation invariant distributions in 𝒟′​(𝕄2\Diag)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}^{2}\backslash\mathrm{Diag}), which correspond in relative coordinates to generic distributions t~γ\widetilde{t}_{\gamma} in 𝒟′​(𝕄\{0})\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}\backslash\left\{0\right\}). The scaling degree of these distributions is given by |E​(γ)|​(d−2)\left|E(\gamma)\right|\left(d-2\right), and we can choose a (possibly unique) extension according to Theorem 7.2. By translation invariance this gives extensions tγ∈𝒟′​(𝕄2)t_{\gamma}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}^{2}).

Now we come to the induction step. For a generic EG subgraph γ⊆Γ\gamma\subseteq\Gamma with nn vertices we assume that the extensions of distributions corresponding to all EG subgraphs of γ\gamma with less than nn vertices have already been chosen. The causality condition 3 then gives a translation invariant distribution in 𝒟′​(𝕄|V⁡(γ)|\Diag)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}^{\left|V(\gamma)\right|}\backslash\mathrm{Diag}) which corresponds to a generic distribution t~γ∈𝒟′​(𝕄|V⁡(γ)|−1\{0})\widetilde{t}_{\gamma}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}^{\left|V(\gamma)\right|-1}\backslash\left\{0\right\}). The scaling degree and hence the degree of divergence of this distribution is completely fixed by the structure of the graph:

div⁡(γ)=|E⁡(γ)|​(d−2)−(|V⁡(γ)|−1)​d,d=dim(𝕄).\mathrm{div}(\gamma)=\left|E(\gamma)\right|\left(d-2\right)-\left(\left|V(\gamma)\right|-1\right)d\,,\qquad d=\dim(\mathbb{M})\,. (89)

We call γ\gamma superficially convergent if div⁡(γ)<0\mathrm{div}(\gamma)<0, logarithmically divergent if div⁡(γ)=0\mathrm{div}(\gamma)=0 and divergent of degree div⁡(γ)\mathrm{div}(\gamma) otherwise. Again by Theorem 7.2 there is a choice to be made in the extension of t~γ\widetilde{t}_{\gamma} in the case div⁡(γ)≥0\mathrm{div}(\gamma)\geq 0.

Let us now come back to the case where derivative couplings are present. The scaling degree of p​S~Γp\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma} fulfills:

sd⁡(p​S~Γ)≤sd⁡(SΓ~)+|p|,\mathrm{sd}(p\widetilde{S}_{\Gamma})\leq\mathrm{sd}(\widetilde{S_{\Gamma}})+|p|\,,

where |p||p| is the degree of the polynomial pp. We can see that pp encodes the derivative couplings appearing in the graph γ\gamma. In the framework of Connes-Kreimer Hopf algebras it is called the external structure of the graph. The presence of derivative couplings introduces an additional freedom in the choice of the extension in each step of the Epstein-Glaser induction and one has to use it to fulfill (88). This relation follows basically from the Action Ward Identity, as discussed in [21, 20]. It can be also seen as a consistency condition implementing the Leibniz rule, see [34].

Let us now remark on the relation of the Epstein-Glaser induction to a more conventional approach to renormalization. Firstly we show, how the EG renormalization relates to the regularization procedure. We are given an EG subgraph γ\gamma with nn vertices and we assume that all the subgraphs with n−1n-1 vertices are already renormalized. Let

𝒟λ​(𝕄n−1):={f∈𝒟⁡(𝕄n−1)|(∂αf)​(0)=0​∀|α|≤λ}\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}(\mathbb{M}^{n-1}):=\{f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{M}^{n-1})\,|\,(\partial^{\alpha}f)(0)=0\,\,\,\forall|\alpha|\leq\lambda\} (90)

be the space of functions with derivatives vanishing up to order λ\lambda and let 𝒟λ′​(𝕄n−1)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\lambda}(\mathbb{M}^{n-1}) be the corresponding space of distributions. Theorem 7.2 tells us that the distribution t~γ∈𝒟′​(𝕄n−1)\widetilde{t}_{\gamma}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{M}^{n-1}) associated with the EG subgraph γ\gamma has a unique extension to an element of 𝒟div⁡(γ)′​(𝕄n−1)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{div}(\gamma)}(\mathbb{M}^{n-1}). An extension to a distribution on the full space 𝒟⁡(𝕄n−1)\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{M}^{n-1}) can be therefore defined by a choice of the projection:

W:𝒟⁡(𝕄n−1)→𝒟div⁡(γ)​(𝕄n−1).W:\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{M}^{n-1})\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{div}(\gamma)}(\mathbb{M}^{n-1})\,.

There is a result proven in [19], which characterizes all such projections:

Proposition 7.4.

There is a one-to-one correspondence between families of functions

{wα∈𝒟|∀|β|≤λ:∂βwα(0)=δαβ,|α|≤λ}\left\{w_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{D}\,|\quad\forall\left|\beta\right|\leq\lambda:\partial^{\beta}w_{\alpha}(0)=\delta_{\alpha}^{\beta},\,\left|\alpha\right|\leq\lambda\right\} (91)

and projections W:𝒟→𝒟λW:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}. The set (91) defines a projection WW by

W​f:=f−∑|α|≤λf(α)​(0)​wα.Wf:=f-\sum_{\left|\alpha\right|\leq\lambda}f^{\left(\alpha\right)}(0)\,w_{\alpha}\,. (92)

Conversely a set of functions of the form (91) is given by any basis of ran⁡(1−W)\mathrm{ran}(1-W) dual to the basis {δ(α):|α|≤λ}\left\{\delta^{\left(\alpha\right)}:\left|\alpha\right|\leq\lambda\right\} of 𝒟λ⟂⊂𝒟′\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}^{\perp}\subset\mathcal{D}^{\prime}.

Let us now define, following [37], what we mean by a regularization of a distribution.

Definition 7.5 (Regularization).

Let t~∈𝒟′​(ℝn∖{0})\tilde{t}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}) be a distribution with degree of divergence λ\lambda, and let t¯∈𝒟λ′​(ℝn)\bar{t}\in\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) be the unique extension of t~\tilde{t} with the same degree of divergence. A family of distributions {tζ}ζ∈Ω∖{0}\{t^{\zeta}\}_{\zeta\in\Omega\setminus\{0\}}, tζ∈𝒟′​(ℝn)t^{\zeta}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), with Ω⊂ℂ\Omega\subset\mathbb{C} a neighborhood of the origin, is called a regularization of t~\tilde{t}, if

∀g∈𝒟λ​(ℝn):limζ→0⟨tζ,g⟩=⟨t¯,g⟩.\forall g\in\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}(\mathbb{R}^{n}):\quad\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow 0}\langle t^{\zeta},g\rangle=\langle\bar{t},g\rangle\,. (93)

The regularization {tζ}\{t^{\zeta}\} is called analytic, if for all functions f∈𝒟⁡(ℝn)f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) the map

Ω∖{0}∋ζ↦⟨tζ,f⟩\Omega\setminus\{0\}\ni\zeta\mapsto\langle t^{\zeta},f\rangle (94)

is analytic with a pole of finite order at the origin. The regularization {tζ}\{t^{\zeta}\} is called finite, if the limit limζ→0⟨tζ,f⟩∈ℂ\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow 0}\langle t^{\zeta},f\rangle\in\mathbb{C} exists ∀f∈𝒟⁡(ℝn)\forall f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{n}); in this case limζ→0tζ∈𝒟′​(ℝn)\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow 0}t^{\zeta}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is called an extension or renormalization of t~\tilde{t}.

For a finite regularization the limit limζ→0tζ\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow 0}t^{\zeta} is indeed a solution tt of the extension problem. Given a regularization {tζ}\{t^{\zeta}\} of tt, it follows from (93) that for any projection W:𝒟→𝒟λW:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{\lambda}

⟨t¯,W​f⟩=limζ→0⟨tζ,W​f⟩∀f∈𝒟⁡(ℝn).\langle\bar{t},Wf\rangle=\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow 0}\langle t^{\zeta},Wf\rangle\,\quad\forall f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\,. (95)

Any extension t∈𝒟′​(ℝn)t\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) of t~\tilde{t} with the same scaling degree is of the form ⟨t,f⟩=⟨t¯,W​f⟩\langle t,f\rangle=\langle\bar{t},Wf\rangle with some WW-projection of the form (92). Since tζ∈𝒟′​(ℝn)t^{\zeta}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) we can write (95) in the form

⟨t¯,W​f⟩=limζ→0[⟨tζ,f⟩−∑|α|≤sd⁡(t)−n⟨tζ,wα⟩​f(α)​(0)].\langle\bar{t},Wf\rangle=\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow 0}\left[\langle t^{\zeta},f\rangle-\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\mathrm{sd}(t)-n}\langle t^{\zeta},w_{\alpha}\rangle\;f^{(\alpha)}(0)\right]. (96)

In general the limit on the right hand side cannot be split, since the limits of the individual terms might not exist. However, if the regularization {tζ,ζ∈Ω∖{0}}\{t^{\zeta},\zeta\in\Omega\setminus\{0\}\} is analytic, each term can be expanded in a Laurent series around ζ=0\zeta=0, and since the overall limit is finite, the principal parts (pp\mathrm{pp}) of these Laurent series must coincide. It follows that the principal part of any analytic regularization {tζ}\{t^{\zeta}\} of a distribution t∈𝒟′​(ℝn∖{0})t\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}) is a local distribution of order sd⁡(t)−n\mathrm{sd}(t)-n. We can now give a definition of the minimal subtraction in the EG framework.

Corollary 7.6 (Minimal Subtraction).

The regular part (rp=1−pp\mathrm{rp}=1-\mathrm{pp}) of any analytic regularization {tζ}\{t^{\zeta}\} of a distribution t~∈𝒟′​(ℝn∖{0})\tilde{t}\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}) defines by

⟨tMS,f⟩:=limζ→0rp⁡(⟨tζ,f⟩)\langle t^{\mathrm{MS}},f\rangle:=\lim_{\zeta\rightarrow 0}\mathrm{rp}(\langle t^{\zeta},f\rangle) (97)

an extension of t~\tilde{t} with the same scaling degree, sd⁡(tMS)=sd⁡(t~)\mathrm{sd}(t^{\mathrm{MS}})=\mathrm{sd}(\tilde{t}). The extension tMSt^{\mathrm{MS}} defined by (97) is called “minimal subtraction”.

To finish this discussion we want to remark on the difference between the Epstein-Glaser procedure and the BPHZ scheme. It is best seen on the example of the rising sun diagram of the φ4\varphi^{4} theory. In the framework of BPHZ, it contains three logarithmically divergent subdiagrams, which have to be renormalized first. In the perspective of EG, however, it is a diagram with two vertices and, hence, contains no divergent subdiagram at all. This way one saves some work computing contributions, which, as shown by Zimmermann [59] cancel out in the end.

We have just seen how to define the nn-fold time-ordered products (i.e. multilinear maps 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}) by the procedure of Epstein and Glaser. An interesting question is whether the renormalized time ordered product defined by such a sequence of multilinear maps can be understood as an iterated binary product on a suitable domain. Recently we proved in [25] that this is indeed the case. The crucial observation is that multiplication of local functionals is injective. More precisely, let 𝔉0​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{0}(M) be the set of local functionals vanishing at some distinguished field configuration (say φ=0\varphi=0). Iterated multiplication mm is then a linear map from the symmetric Fock space over 𝔉0​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{0}(M) onto the algebra of functionals which is generated by 𝔉0​(M)\mathfrak{F}_{0}(M). Then there holds the following assertion:

Proposition 7.7.

The multiplication m:S∙​𝔉0​(M)→𝔉⁡(M)m:S^{\bullet}\mathfrak{F}_{0}(M)\to\mathfrak{F}(M) is bijective (where SkS^{k} denotes the symmetrised tensor product of vector spaces).

Let β=m−1\beta=m^{-1}. We now define the renormalized time ordering operator on the space of multilocal functionals 𝔉⁡(M)\mathfrak{F}(M) by

𝒯r:=(⨁n𝒯n)∘β\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{r}}:=(\bigoplus_{n}\mathcal{T}_{n})\circ\beta (98)

This operator is a formal power series in ℏ\hbar starting with the identity, hence it is injective. The renormalized time ordered product is now defined on the image of 𝒯r\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{r}} by

A⋅𝒯rB≐𝒯r(𝒯r−1A⋅𝒯r−1B),A\cdot_{{}^{\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{r}}}}B\doteq\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{r}}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{-1}}A\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\scriptscriptstyle{-1}}B)\,, (99)

This product is equivalent to the pointwise product and is in particular associative and commutative. Moreover, the nn-fold time ordered product of local functionals coincides with the nn-linear map 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} of causal perturbation theory.

Appendix A Distributions and wavefront sets

We recall same basic notions from the theory of distributions on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be an open subset and ℰ⁡(Ω)≐𝒞∞​(Ω,ℝ)\mathcal{E}(\Omega)\doteq\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}) the space of smooth functions on it. We equip this space with a Fréchet topology generated by the family of seminorms:

pK,m​(φ)=supx∈K|α|≤m|∂αφ⁡(x)|,p_{K,m}(\varphi)=\sup_{x\in K\atop|\alpha|\leq m}|\partial^{\alpha}\varphi(x)|\,, (100)

where α∈ℕN\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{N} is a multiindex and K⊂ΩK\subset\Omega is a compact set. This is just the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets, of all the derivatives.

The space of smooth compactly supported functions 𝒟⁡(Ω)≐𝒞c∞​(Ω,ℝ)\mathcal{D}(\Omega)\doteq\mathcal{C}^{\infty}_{c}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}) can be equipped with a locally convex topology in a similar way. The fundamental system of seminorms is given by [49]:

p{m},{ϵ},a​(φ)=supν(sup|x|≥ν,|p|≤mν|Dp​φa​(x)|/ϵν),p_{\{m\},\{\epsilon\},a}(\varphi)=\sup_{\nu}\big(\sup_{|x|\geq\nu,\atop|p|\leq m_{\nu}}\big|D^{p}\varphi^{a}(x)\big|/\epsilon_{\nu}\big)\,, (101)

where {m}\{m\} is an increasing sequence of positive numbers going to +∞+\infty and {ϵ}\{\epsilon\} is a decreasing one tending to 00.

The space of distributions is defined to be the dual 𝒟′​(Ω)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\Omega) of 𝒟⁡(Ω)\mathcal{D}(\Omega) with respect to the topology given by (101). Equivalently, given a linear map LL on 𝒟⁡(Ω)\mathcal{D}(\Omega) we can decide if it is a distribution by checking one of the equivalent conditions given in the theorem below [57, 46, 35].

Theorem A.1.

A linear map uu on ℰ⁡(Ω)\mathcal{E}(\Omega) is a distribution if it satisfies the following equivalent conditions:

  1. 1.

    To every compact subset KK of Ω\Omega there exists an integer mm and a constant C>0C>0 such that for all φ∈𝒟\varphi\in\mathcal{D} with support contained in KK it holds:

    |u⁡(φ)|≤C​max⁡supx∈Ωp≤k⁡|∂pφ⁡(x)|.|u(\varphi)|\leq C\max_{p\leq k}\sup_{x\in\Omega}|\partial^{p}\varphi(x)|\,.

    We call ‖u‖𝒞k​(Ω)≐max⁡supx∈Ωp≤k⁡|∂pφ⁡(x)|||u||_{\mathcal{C}^{k}(\Omega)}\doteq\max_{p\leq k}\sup_{x\in\Omega}|\partial^{p}\varphi(x)| the 𝒞k\mathcal{C}^{k}-norm and if the same integer kk can be used in all KK for a given distribution uu, then we say that uu is of order kk.

  2. 2.

    If a sequence of test functions {φk}\{\varphi_{k}\}, as well as all their derivatives converge uniformly to 0 and if all the test functions φk\varphi_{k} have their supports contained in a compact subset K⊂ΩK\subset\Omega independent of the index kk, then u⁡(φk)→0u(\varphi_{k})\rightarrow 0.

An important property of a distribution is its support. If U′⊂UU^{\prime}\subset U is an open subset then 𝒟⁡(U′)\mathcal{D}(U^{\prime}) is a closed subspace of 𝒟⁡(U)\mathcal{D}(U) and there is a natural restriction map 𝒟′​(U)→𝒟′​(U′)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(U^{\prime}). We denote the restriction of a distribution uu to an open subset U′U^{\prime} by u|U′u|_{U^{\prime}}.

Definition A.2.

The support supp​u\mathrm{supp}u of a distribution u∈𝒟′​(Ω)u\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\Omega) is the smallest closed set 𝒪\mathcal{O} such that u|Ω∖𝒪=0u|_{\Omega\setminus\mathcal{O}}=0. In other words:

suppu≐{x∈Ω|∀Uopen neigh. of x,U⊂Ω∃φ∈𝒟(Ω),suppφ⊂U,s.t.<u,φ>≠0}.\mathrm{supp}u\doteq\{x\in\Omega|\,\forall U\,\textrm{open neigh. of }x,\,U\subset\Omega\ \exists\varphi\in\mathcal{D}(\Omega),\mathrm{supp}\varphi\subset U,\,\mathrm{s.t.}<\!u,\varphi\!>\neq 0\}\,.

Distributions with compact support can be characterized by means of a following theorem:

Theorem A.3.

The set of distributions in Ω\Omega with compact support is identical with the dual ℰ′​(Ω)\mathcal{E}^{\prime}(\Omega) of ℰ⁡(Ω)\mathcal{E}(\Omega) with respect to the topology given by (100).

Now we discuss the singularity structure of distributions. This is mainly based on [35] and chapter 4 of [1].

Definition A.4.

The singular support sing​supp​u\mathrm{sing\,supp}\,u of u∈𝒟′​(Ω)u\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\Omega) is the smallest closed subset 𝒪\mathcal{O} such that u|Ω∖𝒪∈ℰ⁡(Ω∖𝒪)u|_{\Omega\setminus\mathcal{O}}\in\mathcal{E}(\Omega\setminus\mathcal{O}).

We recall an important theorem giving the criterium for a compactly distribution to have an empty singular support:

Theorem A.5.

A distribution u∈ℰ′​(Ω)u\in\mathcal{E}^{\prime}(\Omega) is smooth if and only if for every NN there is a constant CNC_{N} such that:

|u^​(k)|≤CN​(1+|k|)−N,|\hat{u}({k})|\leq C_{N}(1+|{k}|)^{-N}\,,

where u^\hat{u} denotes the Fourier transform of uu.

We can see that a distribution is smooth if its Fourier transform decays fast at infinity. If a distribution has a nonempty singular support we can give a further characterization of its singularity structure by specifying the direction in which it is singular. This is exactly the purpose of the definition of a wave front set.

Definition A.6.

For a distribution u∈𝒟′​(Ω)u\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\Omega) the wavefront set WF⁡(u)\mathrm{WF}(u) is the complement in Ω×ℝn∖{0}\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\} of the set of points (x,k)∈Ω×ℝn∖{0}(x,{k})\in\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\} such that there exist

  • •

    a function f∈𝒟⁡(Ω)f\in\mathcal{D}(\Omega) with f⁡(x)=1f(x)=1,

  • •

    an open conic neighborhood CC of k{k}, with

    supk∈C(1+|k|)N​|f⋅u^​(k)|<∞∀N∈ℕ0.\sup_{{k}\in C}(1+|{k}|)^{N}|\widehat{f\cdot u}({k})|<\infty\qquad\forall N\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\,.

On a manifold MM the definition of the Fourier transform depends on the choice of a chart, but the property of strong decay in some direction (characterized now by a point (x,k)(x,k), k≠0k\neq 0 of the cotangent bundle T∗​MT^{*}M) turns out to be independent of this choice. Therefore the wave front set WF of a distribution on a manifold MM is a well defined closed conical subset of the cotangent bundle (with the zero section removed).

The wavefront sets provide a simple criterion for the existence of point-wise products of distributions. Before we give it, we prove a more general result concerning the pullback. Here we follow closely [1, 35]. Let F:X→YF:X\rightarrow Y be a smooth map between X⊂ℝmX\subset\mathbb{R}^{m} and Y⊂ℝnY\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. We define the normal set NFN_{F} of the map FF as:

NF≐{(F(x),η)∈Y×ℝn|((dFx)T(η)=0},N_{F}\doteq\{(F(x),\eta)\in Y\times\mathbb{R}^{n}|((dF_{x})^{T}(\eta)=0\}\,,

where (d​Fx)T(dF_{x})^{T} is the transposition of the differential of FF at x.

Theorem A.7.

Let Γ\Gamma be a closed cone in Y×(ℝn​{0})Y\times(\mathbb{R}^{n}\{0\}) and F:X→YF:X\rightarrow Y as above, such that NF∩Γ=∅N_{F}\cap\Gamma=\varnothing. Then the pullback of functions F∗:ℰ⁡(X)→ℰ⁡(Y)F^{*}:\mathcal{E}(X)\rightarrow\mathcal{E}(Y) has a unique, sequentially continuous extension to a sequentially continuous map 𝒟Γ′​(Y)→𝒟′​(X)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\Gamma}(Y)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(X), where 𝒟Γ′​(Y)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\Gamma}(Y) denotes the space of distributions with WF sets contained in Γ\Gamma.

Proof.

Here we give only an idea of the proof. Details can be found in [1, 35]. Firstly, one has to show that the problem can be reduced to a local construction. Let x∈Xx\in X. We assumed that NF∩Γ=∅N_{F}\cap\Gamma=\varnothing, so we can choose a compact neighborhood KK of F⁡(x)F(x) and an open neighborhood 𝒪\mathcal{O} of xx such that F⁡(𝒪)¯⊂int​(K)\overline{F(\mathcal{O})}\subset\textrm{int}(K) and the following condition holds:

∃ϵ>0​s.t.​V≐⋃x∈𝒪{k|(d​Fx)T​k}¯​satisfies ​(K×V)∩Γ=∅.\exists\epsilon>0\ \textrm{s.t.}\ V\doteq\overline{\bigcup\limits_{x\in\mathcal{O}}\{{k}|(dF_{x})^{T}{k}\}}\ \textrm{satisfies }(K\times V)\cap\Gamma=\varnothing\,.

Such neighborhoods define an cover of XX and we choose its locally finite refinement which we denote by {𝒪α}α∈A\{\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in A}, where AA is some index set. To this cover we have the associated family of compact sets Kλ⊂YK_{\lambda}\subset Y and we choose a partition of unity ∑α∈Agα=1\sum\limits_{\alpha\in A}g_{\alpha}=1, supp​gα⊂𝒪α\mathrm{supp}g_{\alpha}\subset\mathcal{O}_{\alpha} and a family {fα}α∈A\{f_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in A} of functions on YY with supp​fα=Kα\mathrm{supp}f_{\alpha}=K_{\alpha} and fα≡1f_{\alpha}\equiv 1 on F⁡(supp​gα)F(\mathrm{supp}g_{\alpha}). Then:

F∗​(φ)=∑α∈Agα​F∗​(fα​φ).F^{*}(\varphi)=\sum\limits_{\alpha\in A}g_{\alpha}F^{*}(f_{\alpha}\varphi)\,.

This way the problem reduces to finding an extension of Fα∗≐(F|𝒪α)∗:𝒞c∞​(Kα,ℝ)→𝒞∞​(𝒪α,ℝ)F^{*}_{\alpha}\doteq(F\big|_{\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}})^{*}:\mathcal{C}^{\infty}_{c}(K_{\alpha},\mathbb{R})\rightarrow\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathcal{O}_{\alpha},\mathbb{R}) to a map on 𝒟Γ′​(Kα)\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\Gamma}(K_{\alpha}). Note that for φ∈Cc​∞​(Kα)\varphi\in C_{c}\infty(K_{\alpha}), supp​χ⊂𝒪α\mathrm{supp}\chi\subset\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}, we can write the pullback as:

⟨Fα∗​(φ),χ⟩=∫φ⁡(Fα​(x))​χ​(x)​𝑑x=∫φ^​(η)​ei​⟨Fα​(x),η⟩​χ​(x)​𝑑x​𝑑η=∫φ^​(η)​Tχ​(η)​𝑑η,\left<F_{\alpha}^{*}(\varphi),\chi\right>=\int\varphi(F_{\alpha}(x))\chi(x)dx=\int\hat{\varphi}(\eta)e^{i\left<F_{\alpha}(x),\eta\right>}\chi(x)dxd\eta=\int\hat{\varphi}(\eta)T_{\chi}(\eta)d\eta\,,

where we denoted Tχ​(η)≐∫ei​⟨Fα​(x),η⟩​χ​(x)​𝑑xT_{\chi}(\eta)\doteq\int e^{i\left<F_{\alpha}(x),\eta\right>}\chi(x)dx. We can use this expression to define the pullback for u∈𝒟Γ′​(Kα)u\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\Gamma}(K_{\alpha}), by setting:

⟨Fα∗​(u),χ⟩≐∫u^​(η)​Tχ​(η)​𝑑η.\left<F_{\alpha}^{*}(u),\chi\right>\doteq\int\hat{u}(\eta)T_{\chi}(\eta)d\eta\,.

To show that this integral converges, we can divide it into two parts: integration over VαV_{\alpha} and over ℝn∖Vα\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus V_{\alpha}, i.e.:

⟨Fα∗​(u),χ⟩=∫Vαu^​(η)​Tχ​(η)​𝑑η+∫ℝn∖Vαu^​(η)​Tχ​(η)​𝑑η,.\left<F_{\alpha}^{*}(u),\chi\right>=\int\limits_{V_{\alpha}}\hat{u}(\eta)T_{\chi}(\eta)d\eta\,+\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus V_{\alpha}}\hat{u}(\eta)T_{\chi}(\eta)d\eta\\ ,.

The first integral converges since Kα×Vα∩Γ=∅K_{\alpha}\times V_{\alpha}\cap\Gamma=\varnothing and therefore u^​(η)\hat{u}(\eta) decays rapidly on VαV_{\alpha}, whereas |Tχ​(η)|≤∫|χ⁡(x)|​𝑑x|T_{\chi}(\eta)|\leq\int|\chi(x)|dx. The second integral also converges. To prove it, first we note that u^​(η)\hat{u}(\eta) is polynomially bounded i.e. φ^​(η)≤C​(1+|η|)N\hat{\varphi}(\eta)\leq C(1+|\eta|)^{N} for some NN and appropriately chosen constant CC. Secondly, we have a following estimate on Tχ​(η)T_{\chi}(\eta): for ever k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and a closed conic subset V⊂ℝnV\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} such that (d​Fx)T​η≠0(dF_{x})^{T}\eta\neq 0 for η∈V\eta\in V, there exists a constant Ck,VC_{k,V} for which it holds88 8 For the proof of this estimate see [1, 35]

|Tχ​(η)|≤Ck,V​(1+|η|)−k,|T_{\chi}(\eta)|\leq C_{k,V}(1+|\eta|)^{-k}\,,

Since for η∈Vα\eta\in V_{\alpha} it holds (d​Fx)T​η>ϵ>0(dF_{x})^{T}\eta>\epsilon>0, we can use this estimate to prove the convergence of the second integral.

We already proved that F∗:𝒟Γ′​(Y)→𝒟′​(X)F^{*}:\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\Gamma}(Y)\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(X) exists. Now it remains to show its sequential continuity. This can be easily done, with the use of estimates provided above and the uniform boundedness principle. ∎

Using this theorem we can define the pointwise product of two distributions t,st,s on an nn-dimensional manifold MM as a pullback by the diagonal map D:M→M×MD:M\rightarrow M\times M if the pointwise sum of their wave front sets

WF(t)+WF(s)={(x,k+k′)|(x,k)∈WF(t),(x,k′)∈WF(s)},\mathrm{WF}(t)+\mathrm{WF}(s)=\{(x,k+k^{\prime})|(x,k)\in\mathrm{WF}(t),(x,k^{\prime})\in\mathrm{WF}(s)\}\,,

does not intersect the zero section of T˙∗​M\dot{T}^{*}M. This is the theorem 8.2.10 of [35]. To see that this is the right criterium, note that the set of normals of the diagonal map D:x↦(x,x)D:x\mapsto(x,x) is given by ND={(x,x,k,−k)|x∈M,k∈T∗M}N_{D}=\{(x,x,k,-k)|x\in M,k\in T^{*}M\}. The product t​sts is be defined by: t​s=D∗​(t⊗s)ts=D^{*}(t\otimes s) and if one of t,st,s is compactly supported, then so is t​sts and we define the contraction by ⟨t,s⟩≐t​s^​(0)\left<t,s\right>\doteq\widehat{ts}(0).
